papers.abstract: Abstractive summarization remains challenging across languages, where linguistic quality and factual consistency may diverge, particularly in low-resource settings. We present a standardized zero-shot benchmark of eight closed-source and open-weight LLMs on size-matched English and Bengali XL-Sum test sets. Our evaluation combines lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, providing a comprehensive analysis of both surface-level quality and factual reliability in multilingual summarization. Results reveal substantial cross-lingual variation: GPT-5.6 Luna leads several English lexical metrics but does not maintain the same advantage in Bengali, where LLaMA 3.3 70B achieves the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores. Gemini 2.5 Flash obtains the highest observed Bengali factuality score. Furthermore, evaluation methods produce different model rankings, highlighting the limitations of relying on a single metric for multilingual summarization assessment. These findings demonstrate that strong English summarization performance does not necessarily transfer to Bengali and emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks for low-resource languages.

papers.title: Anomalies, higher symmetries, and homotopy theory I: crossed precosheaves and a nonabelian Cech construction
papers.abstract: Symmetries of a quantum field theory or a quantum lattice model are expected to be described not by a group but by a homotopy type, whose homotopy groups are the higher symmetry groups and whose Postnikov invariants encode 't Hooft anomalies. We propose a homotopy-theoretic definition of 't Hooft anomalies based on the structure of localized symmetries in the operator-algebraic approach. The input is a crossed precosheaf: a collection of groups attached to regions of space, equipped with pairings recording that the commutator of two transformations localized in two regions is localized in their intersection. To a crossed precosheaf and a finite family of regions we attach a pointed connected homotopy type, the Cech-Loday classifying space. As the family of regions ranges over finite covers of space, the classifying spaces form a pro-object in the homotopy category. There is a canonical map from the ordinary classifying space of the symmetry group to this pro-type. Composing this map with a group action gives an anomaly whose nontriviality obstructs gauging. In favorable cases, the Cech-Loday space is essentially independent of the cover. In such cases, the homotopy fiber of the canonical map is a candidate for the classifying space of the higher group of symmetries. We give examples of crossed precosheaves arising from gauge transformations in continuum field theory and from quantum cellular automata and finite-depth circuits. For quantum spin systems in one and two dimensions, our construction recovers the Else-Nayak index and its generalizations to two dimensions.

papers.title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
papers.abstract: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.

papers.title: Nanoscale Mapping of Strain-engineered Excitons in Monolayer WSe$_2$
papers.abstract: Excitons in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are highly sensitive to external stimuli, allowing control of resonance energies and lifetimes through electric and magnetic fields, heterostructures, moire potentials and mechanical strain. Observations of single-photon emission (SPE) near sample edges, wrinkles, and strained nanobubbles have motivated strain-engineering aimed at realizing localized emitters in 2D materials. The origin of these emitters remains unclear and prior studies have relied on far-field spectroscopy with strain profiles inferred separately through topography, limiting direct correlation between local strain and excitonic response. We directly probe strain-modified excitonic spectra in monolayer WSe$_2$ using cryogenic scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM). We compare two strain-engineering techniques, nano-indentation and patterned substrates, used to produce SPEs. At 9 K, we spatially resolve exciton resonance shifts with sub-diffraction limit resolution, simultaneously measuring near-field optical response and topography. We observe that strain transferred from nano-indentation into a deformable polymer substrate differs from that produced by draping TMDs over patterned dielectric pillars. Adhesion and tearing during plastic deformation drive a compressive exciton blueshift, while draping produces dominant tensile strain. Comparing the strain model results to the experimentally observed energy shifts shows that the nano-indentation strain is over an order of magnitude smaller than previously inferred, due to puncturing of the fragile monolayer, whereas pillar-strained devices remain intact under more modest strain. These differences suggest SPE arises from complex, strain-mediated interactions rather than simple confinement potentials, establishing s-SNOM as a powerful probe of quantum emission in strained 2D materials.

papers.title: Action Jets: Learning the Local Shape of the Action-conditioned Data Manifold
papers.abstract: World models are a powerful means of reasoning and planning, but many of these action-conditioned predictive models are high dimensional and computationally expensive. These challenges limit the number of action candidates that can be evaluated by a planner. We show that this cost is avoidable for planners over short horizons, which only require local information with respect to the current state. For a fixed state, the frames reachable by varying a low-dimensional action (a camera movement or an end-effector command) lie on a low-dimensional manifold. We estimate the local shape of that manifold directly via a network trained to estimate how each image region moves per unit of each action axis supervised by data collected from samples by the generator. A correction head fit to trajectory data estimates the shape of this manifold region up to a third-order Taylor polynomial. We call this network estimating the Taylor polynomial describing the manifold shape an Action Jet and compute its radius of validity in closed form. By traversing this approximation of the local manifold shape, we only have to perform inference once per state for any number of candidate actions. Scoring sixteen candidates from a single extraction is over 300x faster than with either source generator, and this gap widens with the number of candidates a planner evaluates. We measure against state-of-the-art action-conditioned generators, IRASim and WorldGym on BridgeData V2, a real 7-DoF manipulation benchmark, and FrameCrafter on DL3DV scenes, where we chart from the novel-view generators DepthSplat and LagerNVS. Because only the tangent comes from the generator and every other term from the data, the Action Jet also predicts held-out frames more accurately than IRASim, the generator that supplied its tangent, at short horizons and at over 100x less compute.

papers.title: Exponential Stability of Slow--Fast Stochastic Systems with a Small Delay
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the exponential stability of coupled slow--fast stochastic systems with a small delay. Under an averaged Lyapunov condition, we establish practical $p$th-moment exponential stability for $0<p<2$ using a cutoff-function approach to handle singular Lyapunov derivatives near the origin. Exponential stability in the $p$th moment and almost surely is further obtained through two distinct mechanisms: homogeneous dissipation of the fast dynamics or vanishing sensitivity of the slow coefficients to the fast state near the origin. We extend these results to locally Lipschitz systems, establishing exponential stability with arbitrarily high probability for bounded sets of initial data, thereby broadening the applicability of stability analysis for stochastic systems with delayed feedback. Numerical examples illustrate our results.

papers.title: First L-type substellar object discovered in the vicinity of the embedded cluster NGC 2023
papers.abstract: We present the first substellar object in a star-forming region spectroscopically confirmed with Euclid, namely J054158.70-021031.4. This young and faint source is located close to the embedded open cluster NGC 2023. It has a spectral type of L3, a reddening of Av = 3 mag, proper motion consistent with the nearby cluster NGC 2024, and a magnitude of $\sim24.5$ in the Euclid optical band. At the distance of 403 pc, its inferred mass lies close to the planetary-mass boundary. We discovered the object by searching for ultracool dwarf candidates in the Euclid Early Release Observations. The search was based on photometric criteria, followed by the analysis of slitless 2D spectro-images in order to distinguish features that indicate the nature of these objects. This work demonstrates the potential of Euclid to unveil previously hidden populations of very low-mass objects, located in obscured regions where star formation is ongoing.

papers.title: A sharp discrete Sobolev inequality and left inverses of higher order differences
papers.abstract: For integers $α,d \geqslant1$, we determine the best constants in the inequalities $||(a_j)_{j=1}^{d}||_{\ell^1} \leqslant C_{α,d} ||((Δ^αa)_j)_{j=1}^{d+α}||_{\ell^2},$ where $Δ$ is the difference operator. We find that these constants correspond to the $\ell^2$ norm of the discrete Chebyshev polynomials, and show that the extremal sequences may be obtained by appropriate sampling of the discrete Landau polynomials. From beginning to end, this project was carried out without use of AI.

papers.title: PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization
papers.abstract: The Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO) benchmark standardized evaluation in molecular optimization, but it is built on simple property-based oracles that do not capture structure-based drug design. As the field has moved to docking-based objectives, evaluation practice has become unstandardized, and different methods report results on different docking tasks, often without a shared protocol for fair comparison or sample-efficiency constraints. To address this, we introduce Practical Molecular Optimization for Docking (PMO-Dock), a benchmark and protocol for docking-based optimization consisting of 25 tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task requiring strong on-target binding while penalizing off-target interactions. The protocol separates model development from final evaluation: validation tasks are used for hyperparameter tuning, and test tasks are held out for final evaluation and are not used during development. Evaluation on the test tasks is done under a strict oracle budget to reflect realistic drug-discovery settings. We benchmark four diverse high-performing methods spanning different optimization paradigms, Saturn (reinforcement learning), GenMol (discrete diffusion), Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama (LLM-based evolutionary search). Our results show no universally best method across tasks, additional analyses of hyperparameter transfer (cross-task and cross-category) and sensitivity show that transfer is often limited and varies by method, motivating method-dependent selection strategies. This benchmark provides a concrete standard for evaluating generalization to unseen tasks and sample efficiency under a limited test-time oracle budget.

papers.title: On the work of Graeme Segal
papers.abstract: This is my written Laudatio for Graeme Segal on receiving the Chern Medal at the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians. I make some general remarks about Segal's qualities as a mathematician. Then I discuss the origins of his work on classifying spaces of categories and Gamma-spaces. In the last section I describe his axiom system for Wick-rotated quantum field theory and some of his subsequent work in the area. Of course, this is necessarily only a small slice of Segal's total research output.

papers.title: Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Current scaling law formulations suggest that increasing the number of unique samples in a dataset improves model performance, while repeated exposure to the same samples provides diminishing value. In this work, we examine this assumption for image self-distillation models. Through systematic experiments across diverse datasets, namely Maxar, SATLAS, Waymo, nuPlan, Ego4D, ImageNet, and YFCC15M, we demonstrate that the effects of sample repetition on downstream performance are non-trivial and dataset-dependent. We identify settings where repeatedly training on a smaller random subset can outperform training on a larger set of unique samples. This finding highlights a limitation of existing scaling laws. To address this gap, we propose a modified version of a Chinchilla-style scaling law that explicitly accounts for two factors: the number of unique samples and repetition per sample. This formulation provides a framework for understanding data-compute trade-offs and improves prediction in some regimes where repetition plays a central role, although its benefits are not consistent across datasets. Finally, we examine how subset selection and augmentation affect downstream performance.

papers.title: Internal partitions of $5$-regular and $8$-regular graphs
papers.abstract: An \emph{internal partition} of a graph is a partition of its vertex set into two nonempty parts such that every vertex has at least half of its neighbors in its own part. DeVos asked whether, for every fixed positive integer $r$, all but finitely many $r$-regular graphs admit an internal partition. This was previously known to hold only for $r\in\{3,4,6\}$. In this paper, we confirm this for $r\in\{5,8\}$ by proving that every $r$-regular graph on at least $10^7$ vertices has an internal partition.

papers.title: Scaling Cheap Synthetic Pretraining Improves Indoor Radio-Map Prediction
papers.abstract: Real measurements are too limited to train an accurate indoor pathloss predictor that works across a wide range of buildings. Large-scale synthetic pretraining offers a way forward, but real building layouts are also scarce, and accurate ray-tracing simulators are slow, expensive, and often proprietary. We address both problems by introducing a generator that automatically creates diverse indoor layouts and a fast, open-source approximate ray tracer that computes radio maps for them. Using this pipeline, we generate 128M synthetic samples, pretrain ResNet-101 and Swin-T encoder-decoders, and fine-tune them on high-quality benchmark data. Despite simulator mismatch, our ResNet-101 model reduces error by 15% on average relative to the best known methods across five indoor radio-map prediction tasks and improves transfer on a small real-measurement dataset. Both architectures show predictable data-scaling trends: power laws fitted on 2M-16M samples predict the mean normalized downstream RMSE at 32M-128M with 3.33% mean absolute percentage error for ResNet-101 and 7.10% for Swin-T. These results show that pretraining on large amounts of cheap simulated data can improve indoor radio-map prediction, even when real measurements and high-quality simulations are limited.

papers.title: IR-PRM+ with Previous-Utility Prediction: Constant Regret and Best-Iterate Convergence
papers.abstract: Regret matching (and its variants) and counterfactual regret minimization are central algorithms in practice for normal-form and extensive-form game solving. Yet these have historically lacked the stronger theoretical convergence guarantees available to optimistic and extra-gradient methods. Recent work introduced IREG-PRM+, a regret matching variant which does have strong theoretical convergence guarantees. However, it relies on a simultaneous, extra-gradient update. IREG-PRM+ is an instance of the more general IR-PRM framework, where empirically optimistic and alternating updates often have better performance. However, the prior extra-gradient analysis does not extend to these cases. We introduce a new approach that covers both settings. For simultaneous and alternating IR-PRM+ in finite two-player zero-sum matrix games, previous-utility prediction recovers the constant-regret and convergence-rate guarantees previously obtained with extra-gradient prediction: external regret bounded independently of T, an O(T^{-1}) average duality gap, and an O(T^{-1/2}) best-current-iterate gap. Moreover, the current duality gap vanishes and the current profile converges to the Nash equilibrium set. The key step bounds the component of consecutive strategy movement not controlled by the existing IR-PRM+ regret inequality using the relative growth of the nondecreasing regret-vector norm rho_t. Coupling this bound across the two players yields recurrences whose effective coefficient scales as 1/(rho_t^X rho_t^Y), preventing unbounded norm growth. We extend the analysis to finitely many simplex learners under a weighted Minty condition and, through the corresponding CFR variant IR-PCFR+, recover analogous guarantees for finite two-player zero-sum perfect-recall extensive-form games under the same full-reach condition as prior work.

papers.title: Topological superconductivity in layered d-wave altermagnetic metals
papers.abstract: We investigate multilayer d-wave altermagnetic metals with odd-parity helical p-wave pairing. In the minimal bilayer system, interlayer tunneling reconstructs the spin-split Fermi surfaces and generates two layer-hybridized sectors with distinct effective chemical potentials. Without Rashba spin-orbit coupling (RSOC), the emergent mirror symmetry and subsystem chiral symmetry stabilize phases with different numbers of helical Majorana edge-mode pairs and additional counterpropagating pairs, jointly characterized by the mirror Chern number and the winding numbers defined along high-symmetry lines. The combination of RSOC and the altermagnetic exchange field gaps out the helical Majorana pairs while, in a certain parameter regime, leaving another pair of counterpropagating Majorana edge modes gapless, giving rise to second-order topological phases with isolated or twofold Majorana corner modes, as well as a hybrid-order phase in which gapless Majorana edge modes coexist with Majorana corner modes. We identify a layer symmetry that elucidates the physical origin of these phases. For an arbitrary N-layer system, such a symmetry naturally arises from the interlayer-coupling matrix, allowing N-fold Majorana corner modes to emerge when all layer-hybridized sectors enter the nontrivial second-order regime. Our results establish the interplay among the layer degree of freedom, odd-parity pairing, and Fermi-surface configurations as a controllable route to engineering topological superconductivity in layered altermagnetic systems.

papers.title: SPICY 30021: an embedded bona fide FUor with a mid-infrared precursor
papers.abstract: Unstable mass accretion in young stellar objects (YSOs) often leads to observable outbursts, which play a key role in stellar mass assembly during pre-main-sequence evolution. The highest-amplitude, longest-duration events are classified as FUors. Until recently, only 50 FUor events had been confirmed. Many occur in embedded protostars, which are difficult to monitor in optical surveys. We present photometric and spectroscopic observations of SPICY 30021, an eruptive young star discovered in the mid-infrared (MIR) NEOWISE time series. We aim to construct its spectral energy distribution and characterise its eruptive nature. We compiled multi-wavelength photometric time series from NEOWISE, VVV and VVV-RENEW, and obtained photometric and spectroscopic observations during the outburst with SOAR, Magellan and VLT, including data from the ESO public survey VVVX-GalCen. We identified the outbursting source, separated it from nearby companions, and estimated the line-of-sight extinction from spectroscopic features. Stellar parameters were constrained using radial velocity, proper motions and stellar evolution models. SPICY 30021 is an optically obscured FUor with a total interstellar and circumstellar extinction of Av = 12.5 mag. Its spectrum closely resembles those of classical FUors. Multiple methods yield a distance of 1.7+_0.4 kpc. Its accretion luminosity is Lacc = 32 L_sol, moderate among FUors. Quiescent near-infrared photometry is consistent with a young 0.9 M_sol progenitor, although the mass depends on the adopted model and distance. We confirm SPICY 30021 as a bona fide FUor event. Its MIR precursor suggests an outside-in triggering mechanism.

papers.title: Mixing Rates for Analytic Observables: Toral Endomorphisms and Anosov Blaschke Deformations
papers.abstract: We analyze exponential mixing for analytic observables and show that mixing at a double exponential rate occurs for genuinely nonlinear systems. Neither its presence nor its sharp exponent is stable under arbitrarily small area-preserving perturbations in the real-analytic topology. We construct two families of area-preserving Anosov Blaschke product diffeomorphisms that converge in the real-analytic topology to the same hyperbolic toral automorphism. For nonzero parameters, both deformations are topologically conjugate to the linear model but not $C^1$-conjugate. For all nonzero parameter values, the maps in the first family are mixing at a double exponential rate with the same sharp exponent, strictly smaller than that of the linear map. The sharp exponent is therefore not lower semicontinuous at the linear map. In the second family, mixing at a double exponential rate is lost altogether, although the maps remain exponentially mixing. We also establish double exponential bounds for every ergodic toral endomorphism and uniform bounds of the same type for totally ergodic higher-rank toral actions. Our method combines the Fourier escape argument with Koopman operator estimates from a Hilbert space of analytic functions to its dual space of hyperfunctions.

papers.title: Discrete Diffusion Models are Minimax Optimal Under Sparsity
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion models have emerged as a leading alternative to autoregressive models for generating text and other categorical data, yet their theoretical foundations remain less developed than those of their continuous counterparts. For continuous diffusion models, a prominent line of theory suggests that these models can adapt to low-dimensional structure in the data, thereby improving statistical efficiency and generalization. In this work, we investigate the discrete analogue of this phenomenon by studying the statistical rates of discrete diffusion models under sparsity assumptions. By analyzing a nonparametric estimator derived from a regularized score-entropy objective, we establish minimax-optimal rates in the sparse regime. The proposed regularization can be viewed as an adaptation of label smoothing techniques introduced for classification, and does not require the knowledge of the sparsity parameter. This shows that discrete diffusion models can adapt intrinsically to sparsity.

papers.title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?
papers.abstract: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.

papers.title: Sages and Their Anonymous Slips
papers.abstract: Before the game, the sages agree on a finite set of symbols and on a rule for choosing one of them. They are then seated in an unknown order, either in a row or around a circle with a common clockwise direction. Each sage sees only the adjacent sage or sages and secretly writes one symbol. The slips are then mixed, so nobody learns who wrote which symbol; everyone learns only how many times each symbol occurred. The aim is that every sage should be able to independently reconstruct the entire seating. We ask for the smallest number of distinct symbols that makes this possible. We also consider a version in which the seats have fixed public labels, and each sage is told the label of their own seat. For large numbers of sages, the minimum number of symbols is proportional to the square of the number of sages, up to a constant factor. Several small cases can be settled exactly. Four sages in a row need exactly two symbols, and so do five sages on a circle. Six sages on a circle need exactly three symbols, both with and without labeled seats; we give a short explicit rule. Five sages in a row with labeled seats also need exactly three symbols. Without seat labels, two symbols are impossible, and four are sufficient; whether three symbols suffice remains open.

papers.title: A Performative Control Approach to Day-to-Day Traffic Signal Retiming
papers.abstract: Conventional fixed-time traffic signal optimization and recent day-to-day signal retiming generally model route adaptation under prescribed route-choice behavior and origin-destination (OD) demand, while neglecting the fact that travelers' behavior can be performative to the signal control policy. A signal timing policy learned from historical traffic observations must therefore account for how its own deployment changes the distribution on which it will be evaluated in the future. We formulate this problem as performative signal control under observed traveler responses and characterize performative stability of the coupled policy-demand system. We propose incremental day-to-day retiming using the local policy gradient at the current operating point, estimated offline through simulation-based zeroth-order optimization without an explicit day-to-day demand-response model. This gradual approach provides a feasible path for policy and demand to co-evolve toward stability. Experiments on a downtown Denver network show that our approach improves congestion, throughput, and stability, generalizes across different demand levels, and remains effective when the offline simulator contains mismatched travel demand and routing behaviors.

papers.title: Invariant von Neumann subalgebras of crossed products and tensor products
papers.abstract: Let $Γ$ be a countable discrete group acting on a tracial von Neumann algebra $(Q,τ_Q)$ in a trace-preserving way. We study invariant von Neumann subalgebras of $Q\rtimesΓ$ and of $L(Γ)\bar\otimes Q$, where the latter is equipped with the diagonal action. We show that, under the pointwise weak mixing assumption, an invariant subalgebra whose image under the canonical conditional expectation onto $Q$ is scalar is necessarily contained in $L(Γ)$. Further, under relative weak mixing and central freeness assumptions, we determine the structure of invariant subalgebras of the crossed product with non-trivial intersection with $Q$. For p.m.p. actions of groups with trivial amenable radical and the invariant subalgebras rigidity property, pointwise relative weak mixing gives a complete classification of invariant subalgebras in the tensor product case. We construct essentially free, prime, pointwise weakly mixing p.m.p. actions of $\mathbb{F}_n$ for every $2\leq n\leq\infty$, as well as non-prime examples with explicitly described factors.

papers.title: Two-loop $gg\to AA$ amplitudes near threshold and the double parton scattering singularity
papers.abstract: The two-loop amplitudes for pseudoscalar pair production in gluon fusion, $gg\to AA$, with each pseudoscalar emitted from its own effective gluon vertex, are known in closed form, but large cancellations near threshold obscure their analytic structure. We expand the IR-finite amplitudes in the pseudoscalar velocity $β_A$ through $β_A^6$ at fixed scattering angle. All inverse powers of $β_A$ and the odd powers through $β_A^5$ cancel, and at leading power the angular dependence enters only through $\ln(2p_T/m_A)$. We identify this logarithm with the double parton scattering (DPS) singularity: with the overall constant fixed at threshold, the factorisation formula of Gaunt and Stirling reproduces the velocity dependence of its one-loop coefficient in the forward limit to $3\times10^{-15}$, and a one-loop $gg\to HH$ analysis confirms the corresponding CP-even weight. At two loops the equal-helicity amplitude grows as $\ln^3p_T$, with the leading logarithmic ratio of planar $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, while the opposite helicity amplitude, which has no one-loop DPS logarithm, grows as $\ln^2p_T$. In the finite virtual correction, relative to the squared tree amplitude, the highest logarithm at order $α_s^2$ is $-\tfrac{7}{64}α_s^2N_c^2\ln^2(2p_T/m_A)$. For $β_A\leq0.2$ the series reproduce the unexpanded amplitudes with relative errors of at most $6.77\times10^{-5}$ at the tested points; they provide this two-loop contribution to the hard function for soft-gluon resummation of the pair invariant-mass distribution near $m_{AA}=2m_A$ and are released with code for their numerical evaluation.

papers.title: How Far Can Coding Agents Go in Visual Generation?
papers.abstract: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. Our study of zero-shot drawing on AgentDrawBench, a 200-prompt benchmark, reveals a distinctive capability profile. Agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, achieving competitive results in domains where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealistic appearance, while remaining limited in perceptual richness. Their visual expressiveness varies with the drawing interface, and a qualitative study on reconstruction shows how procedural skills extracted from human demonstrations support different artistic media. We then examine code as an external visual language of thought: a structured, executable representation that agents can construct and inspect. We test it in visual question answering task and find reconstructed visual code retains substantial information for question answering and, in some domains, supports higher accuracy than the original image. These abilities raise a further question: do agents draw on a shared internal representation of scene content beyond a particular drawing program? We explore an internal visual language-of-thought hypothesis, in which a shared, compositionally structured representation supports visual operations across drawing languages. Cross-harness drawings and images assembled from independent single-pixel queries exhibit related layouts and tones. Agents also maintain self-generated room arrangements across viewpoints after visible drawings are removed. These results demonstrate that the coding agent would maintain a consistent and coherent world inside its imagine even before the harness gets involved and the generation starts.

papers.title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.

papers.title: Optimization for One, Feasibility for Most: Decoupling Optimization from Feasibility in Chance-Constrained Programs
papers.abstract: Chance-constrained stochastic programs (CCSPs) require solutions that satisfy uncertain constraints with high probability. Standard approaches either embed scenarios directly into optimization by considering sample average approximation (SAA)-based reformulations, growing prohibitively expensive and often failing to find feasible solutions; or employ conservative reformulations that guarantee feasibility but sacrifice objective quality by design. We propose ACCESS (Adaptive Chance-Constrained Exploration via Structured Sampling), a structured sampling framework that decouples optimization from feasibility evaluation. First, high-quality candidate solutions are generated by solving many inexpensive single-scenario subproblems, avoiding sampling directly in the constrained high-dimensional solution space. Second, feasibility is assessed separately via large-scale batched simulation over a massive number of scenarios, which is naturally amenable to GPU parallelism. That reduces the search from a high-dimensional solution space to a two-dimensional parameter space controlling conservatism and scenario diversity; while concentrating on candidates near the feasibility boundary, where high-quality feasible solutions lie. We also introduce a variant, ACCESS($δ$), which provides certified feasibility guarantees with probability $1-δ$. Experiments across three benchmark classes and five scenario distributions show that ACCESS matches or exceeds the best objective found by any method in nearly every setting, while ACCESS($δ$) is empirically feasible on every instance. The conservative reformulations remain several percent worse in objective, and SAA is frequently infeasible while taking an order of magnitude longer on the harder benchmarks.

papers.title: Crossing the Gender Binary: Modelling Gendered Reference in Science Fiction and General Fiction
papers.abstract: Science fiction is widely credited with unsettling gender. This article asks whether that holds at the linguistic level, in how readily gendered reference gives way to its counterpart, a neutral term, or other social category, and whether it separates the genre from general fiction. It does so by masking man/men, woman/women, and person/people across same-period science fiction and general fiction corpora and classifying RoBERTa's five likeliest substitutes by gender. Retention and displacement are permutation-tested over five resampling rounds, and the underlying sentences are read closely. Both corpora cross the gender binary in both directions, but unequally: where woman is masked, the model predicts a masculine term about twice as often as it predicts a feminine term where man is masked. Each mismatch marks a statistical surprise, a word the corpus did not expect there. Against this shared pattern, science fiction shows greater gender permeability than the general fiction corpus, placing man in feminine contexts more often than general fiction while the reverse rate holds steady. Its degendering tendency is stronger too, drawing both gendered terms toward the neutral. Beyond the binary, a masked woman also draws substitutes naming a social category and no gender far more often than a masked man does. In measuring the gender permeability of man, woman, and person in linguistic distribution and testing whether genre changes it, the study gives science fiction studies linguistic evidence for thematic claims and computational literary studies a pipeline applicable to other category vocabularies, such as race and class.

papers.title: Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
papers.abstract: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.

papers.title: The connection between massive galaxies and their dark matter haloes from $z=0.25$ to $z \sim 4$ from the combined COSMOS, XMM-LSS and ECDF-S fields
papers.abstract: Understanding how galaxies populate and grow within dark matter haloes is essential for linking the observed evolution of galaxies to the hierarchical growth of structure. We present a galaxy clustering analysis using optical and near-infrared data from the UltraVISTA and VIDEO surveys covering $9.3$ deg$^2$ across the COSMOS, XMM-LSS and ECDF-S fields, $\sim 5\times$ larger than previous comparable studies, providing sufficient volume to determine the halo occupation of the most massive galaxies to $z\sim 4$. We measure the angular two-point correlation function for stellar-mass-selected galaxies over $0.25<z<4$ and by combining the three fields, we reduce the cosmic variance by a factor of $\sim2$ compared to the individual fields. The stellar-to-halo mass ratio peaks at a halo mass of $M_{h}\approx10^{12} {\rm M}_{\odot}$ and is a maximum at $z\sim 1$. For the most massive galaxies, the peak halo mass ($M_{h}^{\rm peak}$) increases from $z=1\rightarrow 0$, while the peak stellar mass in such haloes remains approximately constant, indicating that at $z<1$ massive galaxy formation becomes less efficient. We also find a steady increase in the satellite fraction since $z\sim 1$, from which we infer that massive halos continue to grow hierarchically while their central galaxies experience suppressed stellar-mass growth. We suggest this is due to the central massive galaxies having their growth controlled by feedback from active galactic nuclei feedback, likely from low-power stochastic radio emission.

papers.title: A basis-set-free reference for the exact exchange-energy density and functional development
papers.abstract: The exact local exchange-energy density, obtained from the Slater potential of the Hartree-Fock exchange hole, is a central ingredient of Becke's B05 and B13 functionals and of many other local hybrids. It is usually evaluated in a Gaussian basis, so the local quantity retains a pointwise basis-set incompleteness error. We describe here a basis-set-free numerical code that solves the Kohn-Sham problem on real-space grids for atoms, diatomics, and polyatomics, and returns the exact local exchange-energy density together with the density, its derivatives, the kinetic-energy density, and the reverse Becke-Roussel hole quantities. Reconstructed from the published record of Becke's non-public NUMOL code, AXEL reproduces numerical atomic references through krypton, scalar-relativistic uranium orbital energies, and Becke's diatomic spectroscopic constants. We then extend the original local-density numerical framework to generalized-gradient and hybrid functionals. Comparisons with the independent adaptive-multiwavelet code MRChem give sub-millihartree agreement for Hartree-Fock and PBE0. The same calculations agree with large Gaussian-basis references to a similar level of accuracy. Atom-centred eXact Electronic Limit (AXEL) is intended as both a basis-set-free numerical reference and a platform for exchange-hole-based density-functional development.

papers.title: Velocity-field estimation techniques for on-disk solar coronal bright fronts (CBFs) and shock-wave propagation
papers.abstract: Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are large expulsions of plasma and magnetic fields from the solar corona into the heliosphere. Coronal shock waves are driven by CMEs, and accurate Solar Energetic Particles (SEP) forecasting requires knowing when and where shocks form, how fast they propagate, and how they interact with the coronal magnetic field. By measuring the speed, geometry and temporal evolution of coronal bright fronts (CBFs), one can create more realistic predictions of SEP onset and intensity at Earth, thus velocity-field estimation techniques supply these critical parameters. High-resolution velocity field maps can provide even deeper insight. Instead of yielding only an overall speed of the front, techniques like FLCT and optical flow can show the spatial distribution of velocities across the entire wave dome or front. These analyses reveal which parts of the front are moving fastest and how the front might be deforming as it expands. Here we discuss a set of practical parameters for Lucas--Kanade, Horn--Schunck, FLCT, and Farneback algorithms, arrived at by combining analytic reasoning with empirical measurements on a single event---and demonstrate the potential of these techniques for on-disk shock-wave propagation during the X1.5-class event that took place 10 May 2022, processed by the wavelet-based Wavetrack technique. A better understanding of how to fine-tune these parameters could improve the precision of algorithms running in pipelines, and is especially valuable where per-event hand-tuning is impractical.

papers.title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. SQUELCH adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, SQUELCH improves over LoRA by 2.2--3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8--1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.

papers.title: Logical gate set tomography
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) can strongly suppress noise, but predicting whether a computation succeeds requires understanding not only how much effective noise persists after QEC, but what form that noise takes. To thoroughly characterize this noise, we introduce logical gate set tomography (``logical GST''). Logical GST produces detailed representations of noisy logical operations that can be used to derive higher-level metrics, such as gate fidelity and diamond distance, and to test for non-Markovian and coherent logical errors. We use logical GST to obtain the first full, self-consistent characterization of a universal single-qubit logical gate set, implemented in the seven-qubit Steane code using Quantinuum System Model H1, a 20-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. In the experimental data from H1, logical GST identified predominantly logical Pauli-stochastic errors, found no evidence of logical non-Markovianity, and detected weak potential signatures of coherent logical error. By contrast, higher-shot datasets generated with Quantinuum's detailed system emulator, identify mechanisms for weak but statistically significant logical non-Markovianity and strong evidence of coherent logical error. Finally, we use logical GST to perform error attribution with the system emulator, revealing how specific physical error sources shape logical error mechanisms.

papers.title: Who Should We Listen to More? Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition for Pluralistic Alignment
papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment needs to accommodate diverse preferences under limited human feedback. Using AI simulators to label preference comparisons reduces annotation costs, but variation in simulation accuracy across individuals can leave some people's preferences poorly represented in training. We study how to allocate human feedback across people to construct training data for pluralistic alignment, and how this allocation affects the trained policy. To make this allocation explicit and controllable, we define a social welfare objective over individual supervision utilities that measure label quality. Each query's marginal welfare gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and application-designated priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (WAPA) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate query gains and individual utilities, then selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain while updating recipient utilities. We prove exact optimality of the acquisition algorithm for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions. Experiments on six Roleplay collections and four OpinionQA regions demonstrate improved supervision and controllable allocation tradeoffs. Policy training on four Roleplay collections improves preference prediction for both seen and unseen individuals. When prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, acquiring human labels for 20% of comparisons recovers 75-86% of the average predictive utility gap between policies trained entirely on AI-generated labels and entirely on ground-truth labels.

papers.title: Panopticum of 3D snake models
papers.abstract: Motivated by the standard 2-dimensional 3-segment snake model, leading to the famous $(2,3,5)$ geometry, we discuss a series of 3-dimensional models of similar snakes. In particular, we seek for rules allowing to steer them exclusively by the two joints, which expects 4-dimensional control freedom. This leads to interesting $(4,9)$ and $(4,10)$ models. Finally, we discuss modifications of the previous snakes which lead to $(4,8)$ models. All of the models open further questions and should be a good baseline for further research.

papers.title: Reversible Higgs Bundles
papers.abstract: We study reversible Higgs bundles on a compact Riemann surface $Σ$ of genus $g\geq 2$, that is, $G$-Higgs bundles $(E,Φ)$ with $(E,Φ)\cong(E,-Φ)$. For a complex reductive group $G$ realized as a self-adjoint subgroup of $GL(n,\mathbb{C})$, we show that if $(E,Φ)$ corresponds to a representation $ρ$ of $π_1(Σ)$, then $(E,-Φ)$ corresponds to $(\overlineρ^{\,t})^{-1}$. As a consequence, the moduli space of reversible Higgs bundles is the fixed locus of an involution of the character variety and carries the structure of a real affine algebraic set. For a connected semisimple group and every topological type, we prove that the reversible locus in the smooth moduli space is a $(B,A,A)$-brane. We then describe reversibility through spectral data: in even rank, for a smooth spectral curve, reversible Higgs bundles correspond to line bundles invariant under the involution $η\mapsto-η$; in odd rank, under natural genericity assumptions for which the spectral curve is nodal, we give a gluing criterion together with an explicit polystability condition. Finally, for $SL(2n,\mathbb{C})$ we construct a relative Fourier--Mukai transform over the regular locus of the Hitchin base and prove that it maps the structure sheaf of the reversible locus to an object whose support is exactly the regular degree-zero $PSp(2n,\mathbb{C})$-locus in the Langlands dual $PGL(2n,\mathbb{C})$-moduli space. This support is of type $(B,B,B)$.

papers.title: Lag: A Mean-Field Optimal Policy for Online Assignment with Reusable Resources
papers.abstract: We study online task assignment with reusable resources. This problem arises in peer reviewer assignment, skill-based call routing, rideshare matching, emergency dispatch, and crowdsourcing: Tasks arrive according to a geometric process and must be immediately assigned to servers that become temporarily busy, yielding rewards that depend on the task-server pair. The goal is to maximize long-run average reward. We cast the problem as a contextual restless multi-armed bandit (CRMAB). We derive an occupancy-measure LP (OCC-LP) that upper-bounds the reward of any work-conserving policy. From its dual we obtain Lag, a closed-form index policy. We introduce a scaling regime in which the number of copies of each server and the number of arrivals per step grow together. This regime yields the first deterministic fluid limit for a contextual bandit. In it, Lag is asymptotically optimal. Finally, we evaluate our algorithms on peer review datasets and call center routing. The Lagrangian index achieves 83-99% of the LP upper bound across all load levels. Moreover, the Lagrangian index policy significantly outperforms the natural greedy assignment scheme, improving reward by up to 12.3% on journal data and 36% on structured synthetic instances.

papers.title: Combining Post-Quantum Cryptography and Quantum Key Distribution: Taxonomy, Constructions, Proofs, Standards, Deployments and Open Problems
papers.abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) address the quantum threat from opposite directions: PQC replaces vulnerable public-key algorithms with schemes believed to resist quantum cryptanalysis, while QKD derives keys whose secrecy rests on physical assumptions rather than computational ones. Because each approach has a distinct failure mode, a growing body of work combines them so that a session key remains secure if either component holds. We first establish the deployed baseline, hybrid classical-plus-PQC key exchange, against which QKD-augmented designs must be judged. We then propose a taxonomy of hybrid PQC-QKD designs along eight dimensions (integration layer, combiner construction, authentication scope and source, QKD topology, trusted entities, key-delivery interface, classical component, and evidence type), and use it to compare published protocols, including Muckle and its successors, MACsec and TLS integrations, and IKEv2 mechanisms standardised in RFCs 8784, 9370, and 9867. We examine key-combiner constructions in light of the KEM-combiner literature and of NIST, ETSI, and ITU-T guidance, and map the security arguments for hybrid PQC-QKD protocols onto a common grid of security model, assumptions, permitted compromise, established guarantee, and limitations. We synthesise deployment evidence from metropolitan and national QKD networks, distinguishing the few testbeds that have run PQC in the key path from pure-QKD deployments, and summarise the standards and policy landscape, including the positions of national security agencies that recommend against relying on QKD alone. We close with open problems: authentication of the QKD classical channel, shared-infrastructure threat models, device certification versus formal proofs, formal verification of hybrid handshakes, and the lack of peer-reviewed deployment economics.

papers.title: A Wideband STAR-RIS Employing Shared-Aperture Polarization Conversion and Diagonal Switching Topology for 6G Applications
papers.abstract: Simultaneously transmitting and reflecting reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (STAR-RIS) enable programmable wave control on both sides of a surface, extending wireless coverage beyond single-sided operation. However, practical STAR-RIS demonstrations in literature have narrow bandwidths, because it is challenging to achieve wideband reflection and transmission simultaneously from the same aperture. To overcome this limitation, a wideband STAR-RIS architecture is proposed based on shared-aperture polarization conversion and diagonal switching topology. Here, multiple resonances enable wideband magnitude responses and mirror-symmetric current reversal maintains $180^{\circ}$ phase difference in both reflection and transmission modes. Accordingly, a diagonal four-branch unit cell configuration is developed, where the tailored top patch directs the received wave either through a pair of blind vias connected by a buried strip to the shared top aperture for reflection, or to the bottom ring patch using a through via for transmission. Based on the proposed design, a 10 by 10 STAR-RIS prototype is fabricated and experimentally characterized. The measured 3-dB bandwidths reach 19.8% in reflection mode and 21.9% in transmission mode. Near-field measurements show average signal enhancements of 19.8 and 22.6 dB for reflection and transmission, respectively, over the wide frequency range of 6.8-8.4 GHz. Far-field measurements further demonstrate average received-power enhancements of 11.2 dB in reflection and 11.9 dB in transmission. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this work presents the first experimentally demonstrated wideband STAR-RIS covering the 7.125-8.4 GHz band within the emerging 6G FR3 spectrum.

papers.title: Tracing Morphology, Semantics, and Divergence in Language Acquisition
papers.abstract: Understanding the dynamics of language acquisition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for uncovering how statistical representations evolve into structured linguistic capabilities. However, most existing studies focus primarily on fully trained models, leaving the developmental trajectory across intermediate training stages largely underexplored. In this work, we leverage intermediate checkpoints from open-source models (e.g., Pythia and OLMo) under teacher-forcing evaluation to systematically investigate language acquisition across training steps and model scales. We focus on four core characteristics: morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects. Our findings reveal that models acquire morphological structures well before semantic embeddings stabilize. Furthermore, we show that training dataset size has a positive impact on divergence recognition, while co-occurrence during pre-training and repetition during inference have a negative impact on divergence recognition and associative link generation.

papers.title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.

papers.title: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT
papers.abstract: Because its binary optimization landscape contains exponentially many local optima, MAX-CUT is highly sensitive to initialization. We study Particle Polynomial Relaxation (PPR), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation possessing an advantageous optimization landscape. We warm-start PPR with Combinatorial Multigrid (CMG), a spectral graph-coarsening method that produces structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time without training data. On \texttt{t2g20} ($n=400$), benchmark instance with known exact optimum, the combined CMG+PPR pipeline reaches $97.5\%$ of optimum on average and $98.4\%$ on the best run. An extended variant with discrete local-search refinement reaches the published optimum on all sixty Biq Mac instances evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. Using a sparse CSR representation, the same approach scales to G-set instances with up to $20{,}000$ vertices reducing memory requirements by up to $3333\times$ while maintaining a consistent improvement over the CMG warm start. Gains are largest on sparse weighted graphs; on dense graphs we complement the pipeline with spectral sparsification.

papers.title: RingNav: Task-Shaped Circular Memory for Visual Heading
papers.abstract: Tiny robots have limited computation and memory, yet visual navigation systems often maintain more state than a task requires. We ask whether persistent memory can instead be shaped by the task. We present \textbf{RingNav}, a \(10.6\)k--parameter visual heading estimator that constrains its memory to the circular manifold \(S^1\). RingNav learns only the turn between consecutive images, while heading is composed directly on the circle. On the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge, RingNav reduces mean absolute turn error by \(27\%\) and accumulated heading error over $4$ sec by \(15\%\) relative to a similarly sized learned-memory model. The structured update also gives exactly zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal. Without fine-tuning, RingNav transfers to real-world drone experiments and continues estimating heading under severe visual degradation. RingNav runs at $27.3$Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and can be deployed on an ultra-low power GAP8 processor at $33.4$Hz.

papers.title: Long Term Pediatric Vaccine Tender Scheduling with Quantity Discounts
papers.abstract: Pediatric vaccine procurement for low- and lower-middle-income countries (LICs and LMICs) requires long-term coordination across heterogeneous vaccine markets, competing stakeholder objectives, and uncertain demand, yet tenders are currently scheduled as a series of independent renewals. We extend the Hypothetically Coordinated Vaccine Market (HCVM) framework to schedule multi-year tenders with flexible lengths and all-unit quantity discounts, and compare three objectives: a balanced coordinatingentity model (UG), a social-benefit model that minimizes missed doses (SB), and a producer profit-maximizing model (MP). Using UNICEF ten-year demand forecasts and 30 demand replications across six discount scenarios, we find that the procurement objective, not demand variability, drives cost-to-tender and schedule complexity. Quantity discounts favor large producers, concentrating the market and increasing supply chain vulnerability. Discount effectiveness depends on market maturity rather than valency: pentavalent and hexavalent vaccines are already near their price floor, and among monovalent vaccines only rotavirus responds to discounts, whereas HPV and PCV remain too expensive to compete. Removing pentavalent and hexavalent vaccines from the procurement pool sharply increases missed doses. These results give planners practical guidance on objective selection, discount design, and protecting access to combination vaccines.

papers.title: What Information Buys in Active Inference
papers.abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.

papers.title: TOMOS: Eliminating Data Duplication in Mixed-Precision Matrix Computations
papers.abstract: Mixed-precision algorithms exploit reduced-precision hardware, however computing with the same matrix at distinct precisions typically requires duplicate storage, repeated conversions, or operation-emulation. We introduce TOMOS, a composite-precision matrix format that provides implicit 32-bit and 16-bit access from a single representation. Each FP32 entry is split into a 16-bit primary word for low-precision computation and a complementary word that enables exact FP32 reconstruction. The encoding scheme improves numerical quality of the low-precision view through subnormal representations, and allows exact recovery of high-precision inputs. TOMOS uses FP32-sized storage, with data movement scaling with compute precision. Optimized GEMM and GEMV kernels achieve throughput comparable to vendor libraries on NVIDIA A100 GPUs, while a mixed-precision least-squares solver achieves up to 1.6x speedup over FP32 without redundant matrix allocations.

papers.title: Pre-Trained Language Models as Zero-Shot Tools for Social Science Research
papers.abstract: Record linkage and demographic inference from names are routine demands in social science. Most approaches to these problems require labeled training data that are difficult or costly to acquire. I show that pre-trained language models perform both tasks accurately without requiring task-specific training. For record linkage, I introduce EnsembleLink, an algorithm that uses pre-trained embeddings alongside string-based scorers to retrieve a short list of candidates and then identify the likeliest matches. EnsembleLink matches or exceeds the performance of most prior approaches while generalizing across scripts and formats that those methods are unable to handle. For ethnicity inference from names, I show that large language models (LLMs) achieve up to 83.8% accuracy on U.S. voter files, compared to 78.0% for name-supplemented BISG. Open-weight models offer reproducible implementations that approach these models in accuracy. Moreover, LLMs are able to infer group membership for religious, caste-based, and other ethnic group categories outside of the United States, and reduce bias in downstream estimates of geographic racial gaps. Where pre-training encodes the world knowledge required by each task, task-specific labels add less information.

papers.title: The Atacama Cosmology Telescope: DR6 Constraints on Isotropic Time-Dependent Cosmic Birefringence from Axion-like Particles
papers.abstract: Axion-like particles (ALPs) with sufficiently low masses are dark matter candidates because they could account for much or all of the observed dark matter energy density and help explain observations of galactic substructure. Such pseudoscalar fields could couple to photons, causing a time-dependent rotation of the polarization of the light with an oscillation frequency equal to the ALP mass. We use measurements of the polarization of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) by the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) between 2017 and 2022 to search for this effect using an EB power spectrum estimator. By probing oscillation periods from days to years, the data constrain the coupling between ALPs and photons for ALP masses between $2.5\times 10^{-23}$ eV and $4.8\times 10^{-20}$ eV. We find no evidence for such a signal and set a 95% upper bound on the axion-photon coupling constant, $g_{φγ} < 1.1\times10^{-11}\left({m_φ}/{10^{-21}\,\mathrm{eV}}\right)\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-1} .$ This limit assumes that ALPs make up all of the dark matter and that the ALP field amplitude is stochastically distributed, which leads to more conservative bounds than the deterministic-field assumption used in some previous CMB polarization analyses. Among searches for ALP-photon coupling using CMB polarization, we set the strongest bounds to date under the stochastic-field assumption. This work develops a methodology to analyze over 10,000 time-sliced "depth-1" polarization maps from ACT, a data product that will be standard for time-domain astrophysics with the Simons Observatory, enabling searches with a higher sensitivity and observing span.

papers.title: Focus, Align, and Diffuse: Time-Series-Aware Keyframe Diffusion for Cardiac Dynamic Synthesis from Sparse Observations
papers.abstract: Dense cardiac dynamics are essential for assessing cardiac function, yet in practice clinicians often observe only extremely sparse measurements. However, recovering full dynamics from such sparsity is a highly ill-posed problem due to the lack of temporal cues. While auxiliary time-series signals like ECG provide physiological guidance, effectively exploiting them is challenging due to the cross-modal representation gap and phase misalignment. In this work, we present CardioFAD, a Focus--Align--Diffuse paradigm that reformulates sparse cardiac dynamic synthesis as a recoverability--alignability anchor discovery problem. Our core insight is that resolving extreme temporal ambiguity requires a compact set of anchor states that are both sufficient to recover the visual trajectory and reliable for ECG--visual alignment. We therefore learn motion-salient keyframes under two complementary principles: trajectory sufficiency, which preserves trajectory-critical intra-modal motion content, and anchor alignment, which promotes consistent inter-modal correspondence at these anchors. We implement the Focus and Align modules optimized by the two aspects. Diffuse then performs two-stage generation by first synthesizing keyframes and subsequently interpolating the remaining frames. Extensive experiments on cardiac MRI and echocardiography videos demonstrate superior visual quality, temporal coherence, and improved functional consistency under the extreme one-shot regime.

papers.title: Smart Alone, Blind Together: Why Accuracy Fails to CertifyTheory of Mind in Multi-Agent Teams
papers.abstract: Coordinators that act on what they infer about teammates are usually certified by the accuracy of those inferences. We argue that accuracy is the wrong certificate, for two reasons. First, the accuracy needed to act depends on what a wrong action costs, so the bar belongs to the deployment, not the module. Second, a module's errors are rarely independent, and dependence has a sign: positively associated errors help where their damage overlaps and hurt where it compounds, so an accuracy threshold fails in a predictable direction, and once wrong beliefs interact and can do harm, no rule based on accuracy is right for every module. We test these predictions in task assignment, Level-Based Foraging and Hanabi, with injected errors, trained and Bayesian modules and five language models, and in human judgments. Accuracy fails in both directions, approving harmful language-model deployments in Hanabi, where shared errors compound, and rejecting beneficial ones in task assignment, where costly errors are rare. In our tasks it also buys far less redundancy than independence predicts: from GPT-5.4-mini to Claude Opus 5.5, error on teammates the models have evidence about falls from 32% to 11%, but the chance that all three observers misread one falls only from 16% to 9% (independence: 3.4% to 0.15%). We propose certifying the deployment, with a Blind-Spot Gate that prices error costs, pairwise interactions and measured dependence without deploying the module. On held-out data from the cells it was developed on, it makes no significant false approval in 20 splits (accuracy: 3.2 per split), and in preregistered tests on modules it was not developed on, it recovers what accuracy rejects (seven classifiers: regret 0.004 against 0.479) and catches what accuracy approves (a Bayesian module: significant false approvals in 17 of 20 splits for accuracy, 1 for the gate).

papers.title: Why Do VLMs Fail at Remote Physiological Measurement? Rethinking with Physiological Grounding and Numerical Alignment
papers.abstract: Video-based remote physiological measurement (RPM) has broad applications, while Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide a promising opportunity to enable end-to-end physiological monitoring for future human-aware intelligent systems. However, existing RPM methods rely on task-specific models and cannot be seamlessly integrated with the multimodal understanding and interaction capabilities of VLMs. We revisit RPM with VLMs and provide empirical evidence for two major bottlenecks: generic visual semantic representations fail to preserve fine-grained physiological cues; while discrete token prediction in autoregressive generation is inherently misaligned with continuous numerical measurement. To address these challenges, we propose VITAL (Visual-physiological Token Alignment for Language Models), a visual-physiological token alignment framework for RPM and preserving general vision tasks. VITAL retains the original visual pathway for semantic understanding and introduces an independent physiological pathway to jointly model semantic and physiological information. Moreover, we propose a structured numerical alignment approach to improve the reliability of generative heart rate estimation by enhancing numerical relationship modeling. Extensive experiments show that VITAL improves cross-domain estimation performance on multiple rPPG datasets while preserving the general visual understanding capability of VLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness as a unified visual-physiological model. Code will be released.

papers.title: Deep Generative Models for Phylogenetic Inference with Complex Evolutionary Processes
papers.abstract: Inference of phylogenetic trees from sequences plays a central role in understanding evolutionary relationships, with applications ranging from tracking pathogen spread to reconstructing the history of life. Conventionally, practitioners obtain posteriors over trees using likelihood-based methods like MCMC. However, likelihoods are only available for simple evolutionary models with restrictive assumptions. For realistic evolutionary models, inference using conventional methods is prohibitively expensive, inaccurate, or even impossible. In practice, practitioners settle for using as flexible a conventional method as possible, even though they expect it is misspecified. In principle, we could use simulation-based inference: simulate tree and sequence data from an evolutionary model and train a neural network to predict the posterior over trees given sequences. However it is a mathematical challenge to represent and train complex posterior distributions over trees. Here we present a flexible family of conditional generative models over trees. Our models iteratively build trees using three natural paradigms -- top-down, middle-out, or bottom-up -- and are trained using a discrete diffusion framework. For real and synthetic datasets of up to $65$ taxa and $>10^5$ tokens, our models recover MCMC posteriors much more accurately than the previous state-of-the-art simulation-based method Phyloformer 2. Finally, we compare to IQ-Tree, a popular flexible-but-misspecified conventional method. Our models match its tree estimates on simple data, but on more realistic data, our method is reliably more accurate.

papers.title: The Generalized BEADS Representation: An Informationally Complete Visualization of Mixed Quantum States
papers.abstract: A deep understanding of quantum information theory is essential for quantum science and technology. However, quantum mechanics and particularly quantum information theory suffer from a lack of intuitive images. Visualization tools offer novel perspectives on many problems in quantum physics by revealing important properties of quantum states and processes that are otherwise obscured by abstract mathematical formalisms. Here, we extend the previously established BEADS representation of pure states to the so-called generalized BEADS representation of mixed quantum states. We introduce spherical functions, so-called beads to visualize correlation structures of mixed quantum states. A recursive optimization scheme is used to obtain minimum-entanglement pure state decompositions of all subsystems of a given N-qubit state. We show how correlation function components can be decomposed into individual contributions that directly correspond to different types of correlations of mixed states. This allows us to visually characterize the total correlation, genuine n-partite entanglement, nonclassical quantum-discord-type correlations as well as classical correlations. After outlining the mathematical details relevant for constructing the representation, we examine the generalized BEADS representations for various classes of mixed states including product, classically correlated, separable but nonclassically correlated, as well as entangled states. As exemplary applications of the generalized BEADS representation, we showcase entanglement distillation and the effects of noise channels.

papers.title: Photoemission study of Iodoalkanes
papers.abstract: Core level atomic photoionization is influenced by the molecular environment of the emitting atom.
