This paper {presents a large-scale static quality profiling of} LLM-generated Python code, with a focus on maintainability and reliability. Using 65{,}663 programs from 73 models in LiveCodeBench, we evaluate generated code with established static analysis tools, including Pylint, Radon, and SonarQube. Our results show systematic differences across models that are not captured by correctness alone, with maintainability emerging as the clearest source of variation. We further find that correctness often comes with structural trade-offs rather than uniformly simpler solutions. Overall, our findings motivate evaluation frameworks that assess LLM-generated code beyond pass rates alone.

papers.title: Symmetry-selected extreme shear compliance in a stable carbon monolayer
papers.abstract: Extreme stiffness contrasts between loading modes usually require architected metamaterials with compliant hinges, whereas covalent crystals rarely exhibit such behavior intrinsically. Here, density functional theory calculations of the complete in-plane elastic tensors of four tetragonal carbon monolayers reveal a more than 50-fold spread in shear stiffness, despite less than a twofold variation in axial stiffness and the same symmetry-allowed tensor form. Twin T-graphene shows the strongest contrast: its shear constant, $C_{66}=3.03$~N m$^{-1}$, is 47 times smaller than in graphene and yields a shear Kelvin eigenvalue 29 times below the two normal-strain eigenvalues, while the Born stability criteria hold. This shear constant revises an earlier inference of elastic isotropy based on normal strains alone. Constrained relaxations and symmetry-resolved mode analysis identify the mechanism as a $B_{2g}$ counter-torsion of the carbon sublayers about the mid-plane bonds, which removes 96.3% of the clamped-ion shear stiffness with bond-length changes below 0.15%. An internal-coordinate model quantifies this cancellation, identifying internal relaxation, rather than weak bonding, as the origin of the soft channel. The resulting anisotropy predicts transverse sound velocities of 1.95 km s$^{-1}$ along [100] and 10.62 km s$^{-1}$ along [110], a testable acoustic signature. Phonon calculations, ab initio molecular dynamics at 300 K, and large-deformation simulations indicate that the soft channel is dynamically stable, preserves the local bonding, and persists beyond the harmonic regime. Our results show how bonding topology enables extreme mode-selective elasticity through internal relaxation in a mechanically stable covalent crystal.

papers.title: Verification Turns Capability Gaps into Routing Decisions: Small Language Models for Clinical Documentation
papers.abstract: Clinical note generation from doctor--patient dialogue is high-volume and hallucination-intolerant: a fabricated laboratory value can create patient-safety risk, not a quality regression. We ask whether an agentic \emph{verification} architecture, rather than generator scale, can make a small language model viable here. Holding a four-evaluator verification stack and refinement policy fixed and swapping only the generator between a 4B-parameter model with a QLoRA adapter and a frontier baseline, the small model reaches $0.984$ claim-level factual entailment against $0.992$ and comes within $3.3$ points on completeness, generating entirely on-device. Its deficit is confined to \emph{inter-section structural fidelity}---arrangement rather than clinical comprehension, and the axis on which it also falls furthest below the corpus's reference notes. Because that deficit is an explicit verifier decision rather than a silent quality difference, it becomes a routing policy: run the small model by default, escalate what the verifier rejects. Measured end to end, that it achieved a similiar verified-rate acceptance to the frontier-only acceptance in this test set ($99.6\%$ vs.\ $98.4\%$ over $250$ encounters) while routing $62$, documenting three quarters without a frontier \emph{generation} call. Ablating the loop separates architecture from scale: unrefined, the small model is accepted on $26.8\%$ of encounters and the frontier model on $74.8\%$, so verification does the most work where the generator is weakest. We also contribute section-scoped refinement, which preserves unflagged sections by construction rather than instruction, and find the baseline is not uniformly stronger---its provider refused two trauma-related transcripts the on-device model handled and certified, one facet of a provider dependency a served adapter does not carry.

papers.title: Homological reduction of Courant algebroids
papers.abstract: We develop a homological model for hamiltonian reduction of Courant algebroids, parallel to the BFV formulation of hamiltonian reduction in symplectic geometry. To a hamiltonian action on a Courant algebroid, we associate a differential graded Courant--Dorfman algebra, obtained from the BFV algebra of the corresponding graded symplectic manifold; under usual regularity assumptions, its cohomology recovers the Courant--Dorfman algebra of the reduced Courant algebroid.

papers.title: A direct theory of strain-gradient special Cosserat rods via the principle of virtual work
papers.abstract: Motivated by recent advances in the synthesis of effective one-dimensional mechanical metamaterials, we develop a direct theory of strain-gradient special Cosserat rods based on the principle of virtual work. The internal virtual work is formulated intrinsically in terms of variations of the classical Cosserat strains and their spatial derivatives, without requiring a three-dimensional parent material or being restricted to elastic materials. Objectivity and insensitivity to rigid virtual displacements characterize the admissible internal-work density, while localization yields the dynamic field equations, higher-order contact interactions, natural boundary conditions, and balances of linear and angular momentum. For inextensible and unshearable rods, the constrained principle determines a unique multiplier functional, although its representation by reactive force and double-force fields possesses a gauge freedom absent from classical rod theory. We also formulate objective elastic, hyperelastic, and viscoelastic constitutive laws, extend transverse hemitropy, transverse isotropy, and flip symmetry to strain-gradient rods, and derive invariant representations of symmetric stored energies. As an application, we analyze a planar inextensible cantilever subjected to a compressive terminal force, with stored energy depending on the spatial derivative of curvature. We prove that the eigenvalues of the linearized problem are simple and coincide precisely with the loads at which bifurcation from the straight state occurs. In addition, each bifurcation point generates a connected global branch of nonlinear equilibria that is locally analytic near its origin.

papers.title: One-Loop Renormalization of Spin-$1/2$ SOPHIES
papers.abstract: In this paper, three formulations of spin-$1/2$ Second-Order Pseudo-Hermitian quantum field theorIES (SOPHIES) are built from scratch from parity eigenstates. Pseudo-Hermiticity allows the unconstrained fields to satisfy either Fermi--Dirac or Bose--Einstein statistics, while self-conjugate Majorana-like fields are only compatible with Fermi--Dirac. The set of independent four dimension renormalizable self-interactions of the three theories are identified, and the one-loop renormalization of the unconstrained fermionic and bosonic theories coupled to an abelian gauge boson and enhanced with a Pauli term and including self-interactions is studied, together with the one-loop renormalization of the only independent quartic self-interaction of self-conjugate fields. The analysis leads to a rich set of Renormalization Group Equations with deep connections to known theories, like the Dirac formalism and the Klein--Gordon scalar through the fixed points of the Pauli coupling.

papers.title: Perceptual Characterization of Scan-induced Artifacts in Dynamic 3D Meshes
papers.abstract: Dynamic meshes reconstructed from real-world scenes often exhibit scan-induced artifacts such as surface jitter and missing geometry, which strongly impact perceived visual quality. Objective assessment remains challenging due to the absence of artifact-free ground truth and limited perceptual understanding of artifact interactions. This paper presents a systematic and controlled perceptual study of scan-induced artifacts in dynamic meshes, focusing on surface jitter and holes. To enable systematic analysis, we introduce a physically grounded artifact synthesis framework in which holes are synthesized using a reconstruction uncertainty model derived from multi-view geometry. The study reveals asymmetric cross-artifact interactions, non-additive integration, and motion-dependent temporal masking. Based on these findings, we propose a compact, perceptually grounded no-reference quality assessment framework that encodes the observed perceptual mechanisms.

papers.title: Majority and Torus Polynomials: Bounded-Lift Lower Bounds and Explicit Constructions
papers.abstract: Bhrushundi et al. (2019) introduced torus polynomial approximation as an approach to separating Majority from $ACC^0$. In this model, approximation is measured modulo integers. Krishan and Vishwanathan (2026) developed a duality framework for lower bounds and posed five open problems. We resolve two of these, concerning integer lifts and explicit polynomial approximations. An integer lift records the integer shifts that turn a torus approximation into an ordinary real approximation. We show that a degree-d torus polynomial approximating Majority with error at most 1/8 and lift contained in an interval of width $B$ must satisfy $d(B + 1) = Ω(n)$. This rules out low-degree approximating polynomials with lifts in {-1, 0, 1}, answering their Open Problem 2. We also answer Open Problem 5 by giving, for every Boolean function on $n \geq 1$ variables, an explicit torus polynomial approximation of degree at most $n - 1$. Its error is optimal: zero when the accepting set has even cardinality and $2^{-n-1}$ otherwise. The results presented were discovered and formalized in Lean using GPT-6 Astra.

papers.title: Even and Odd Integer Values of the Secondary Zeta Function
papers.abstract: The secondary zeta function is defined by $$ Z(s)=\sum_{γ>0}\frac{1}{γ^{s}}, $$ where $\tfrac12+iγ$ runs over the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function with positive ordinate, and the Riemann hypothesis is assumed throughout. In this article, we derive convergent integral representations of $Z(s)$ at positive even and odd integer argument, expressed through a differential operator acting on the logarithm of the Riemann $ξ$-function. Define $$ L(x)=\log\left(\frac{ξ(x+\tfrac12)}{ξ(\tfrac12)}\right), \qquad \mathcal{E}=x\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}, \qquad \mathcal{D}_k=\mathcal{E}\prod_{j=1}^{k}(\mathcal{E}-2j). $$ Then, for $k\geq1$, $$ Z(2k)=\frac{(-1)^k}{2^k(k-1)!}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathcal{D}_k L(x)}{x^{2k+1}}\,\mathrm{d}x $$ and $$ Z(2k+1)=\frac{(-1)^k}{π\,(2k-1)!!}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathcal{D}_k L(x)}{x^{2k+2}}\,\mathrm{d}x. $$ In the last part, we write these formulas out explicitly for $Z(k)$, $2\leq k\leq 7$, both in terms of $L(x)$ and in terms of $ξ(x+\tfrac12)$ for reference. We also derive a limit formula for $γ_1$, the ordinate of the first nontrivial zero, and demonstrate its convergence numerically.

papers.title: Learning from Self-Generated Responses: Reliability--Uncertainty Self-Distillation for Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reference solutions and question-specific rubrics are not always available to guide the teacher in self-distillation. A large language model's own solution attempts offer an alternative, but their quality is difficult to assess in open-ended tasks without automatic correctness checks, and even correct attempts can involve uncertain token predictions. We propose Reliability--Uncertainty Self-Distillation (\method{}) to learn from these attempts. The same model serves as teacher and student: the teacher receives the question and completed attempt, and the student matches the teacher's token-level predictions using a question-only prompt. \method{} weights each attempt's distillation loss by additively combining judged reliability, estimated from a self-judge's score and confidence, with student predictive uncertainty. Across eleven reasoning benchmarks, \method{} outperforms all five baselines in average accuracy, reaching 70.47\% on Qwen3-4B and 76.69\% on Qwen3-8B (8.90 and 2.10 percentage points above the base models). Data and code are available at https://github.com/JP-25/RUSD.

papers.title: Multi-System Cognitive Steering for Generative Communication
papers.abstract: A fundamental bottleneck for translating thoughts to speech is the high physical cost of motor input forcing a strict tradeoff between communication speed and expressivity. Generative AI offers a promising solution by expanding highly abbreviated text input into fluent sentences, significantly reducing the motor burden on the user. However, sparse inputs are inherently ambiguous; without sufficient context, AI models frequently misinterpret these abbreviations and generate outputs that fail to align with the user's true cognitive intent. We propose \textit{Cognitive Steering}, a framework that can be leveraged to reconstruct user intent by grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) in multimodal context and applying AI control methods. We demonstrate that aligning frontier models with selected environmental referents, emotional states, and communication motives on simulated abbreviation benchmarks achieves up to $\sim$88\% top-5 expansion accuracy, doubling no-context baselines. We also reveal that different types of context require distinct AI control techniques: while physical objects in a scene are best provided through explicit text prompts, abstract factors like emotion may be more effectively managed by directly altering the AI's internal activations. These findings suggest a hybrid architecture for future interfaces that leverage Cognitive Steering to help users communicate both quickly and accurately, recruiting multiple AI control methods simultaneously to perfectly capture their intended communication goals.

papers.title: Diagnosing Low-Confidence Patient Profiles via Localized Harmful Covariate Shift Detection
papers.abstract: Before deploying clinical prediction models, their reliability must be assessed to ensure safe use. Errors may arise from distribution shifts between training and deployment or from heterogeneous performance where the model systematically underperforms for certain patient subgroups. Yet most post-hoc diagnostic methods evaluate reliability only at the population level, checking whether the deployment data resemble the training data and whether the model performs well on average, without accounting for heterogeneity that may cause some patients to be disproportionately affected. We propose a unified diagnostic pipeline that combines both perspectives. MED3pa first discovers interpretable low-confidence patient profiles, and Detectron is then applied within each profile to test whether its degradation is associated with a detectable harmful covariate shift. Across three clinical prediction tasks and three injected subgroup shifts in MIMIC-IV, we find that shift detectability itself is informative. An injected age shift, undetectable at the population level, was nonetheless localized to specific degraded profiles, whereas sex- and race-related shifts were detected broadly and therefore offered little guidance for identifying the most affected patients.

papers.title: Learning in Strategic Queuing with Geometric Recharge: From Bandits to Systems
papers.abstract: We study packet routing in queuing systems where queues act as selfish, myopic agents that use no-regret learning algorithms to select servers with unknown service rates. To model the small buffers used in data centers, we assume that each server has a single-packet buffer. Even such a tiny buffer already captures the features of buffering: routers can exploit multiple servers while accepted packets remain in service, but packets can occupy servers for multiple rounds, complicating future service and learning. We first analyze a single queue routing packets to $m$ buffered servers with service rates $μ_1, \dots, μ_m$. This setting is equivalent to an instance of the recharging bandits problem with geometric recharge. We prove that any no-regret learner achieves a long-run average throughput of at least the Hamacher sum of the server rates, and that this bound is tight. Consequently, a single no-regret queue is stable if and only if its arrival rate is below the Hamacher sum of the server rates. Moreover, comparing against an optimal policy, we show that any no-regret learner is at least $0.77$-competitive, which is also tight. We then study multi-queue systems where $n$ queues with arrival rates $λ_1, \dots, λ_n$, each at most $λ_{\max}$, compete for service from $m$ buffered servers. We show that the smallest overprovisioning factor that guarantees the system to be stable under high-probability no-regret learning is $\frac{1}{1-λ_{\max}}$. Equivalently, in terms of the total arrival and service rates, the condition $\sum_{i=1}^n λ_i < (1-λ_{\max})\sum_{j=1}^m μ_j$ is sufficient, and sometimes necessary, for stability under no-regret learning. In particular, for $λ_{\max} = 1/2$, this improves the upper bound of Abel et al. (EC 2026) from $3$ to $2$, matching their lower bound and resolving their open question.

papers.title: Cavity-assisted dynamic nuclear polarisation
papers.abstract: Dynamic nuclear polarisation transfers polarisation from electron to nuclear spins by relying on a dissipative channel. Here we introduce a cavity-based DNP mechanism which uses the radiative relaxation of the electronic spin through the Purcell effect to bring about the nuclear spin polarisation. We implement this protocol on an ensemble of bismuth donor spins (I=9/2, S=1/2) in isotopically purified silicon coupled to a superconducting resonator. A single cycle, combining adiabatic microwave and radio-frequency pulses with Purcell relaxation, increases a target ground state's population by a factor of $1.79\pm0.04$; a cumulative enhancement of $4.6\pm0.2$ is reached with additional cycles, to be compared with the theoretical limit of ninefold set by the degeneracy of the ground manifold. We explain this difference by the competition between Purcell and intrinsic relaxation on the one hand and a collective effect that slows down the electronic spin radiative decay as the nuclear spin population grows on the other hand. Our results place radiative DNP as an available mechanism at millikelvin temperatures where phonon-mediated relaxation is frozen.

papers.title: Aggregated Column Generation for Two-Stage Stochastic Mixed-Integer Programs
papers.abstract: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation applied to two-stage stochastic mixed-integer programs (SMIP) has been shown empirically to yield a formulation with strong bounds that can be solved via column generation. However, the time to solve the restricted master problem grows significantly with the number of scenarios due to the increasing number of nonanticipativity constraints (NACs). Moreover, the associated high-dimensional dual space can cause the dual multipliers to oscillate between iterations, further slowing convergence. We propose an aggregated column generation framework for solving a Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation. Applied to SMIP, this method partitions the NACs into groups and replaces each group with a weighted surrogate constraint, leading to a reduced size and providing implicit stabilization by restricting the dual space. While aggregation leads to a relaxation, we develop two strategies for recovering the standard Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation bound. The first iteratively refines the partition by splitting groups that contain violated constraints. The second keeps the partition fixed and adaptively updates the aggregation weights. We prove convergence of the two approaches and study their computational performance on two benchmark problem classes.

papers.title: Galactic Outflows and Star-Formation Quenching: A JWST Perspective
papers.abstract: Outflows driven by active galactic nuclei (AGN) are widely considered a key mechanism for regulating and quenching star formation in massive galaxies. However, direct observational evidence linking outflows to quenching has remained elusive for decades. This article reviews recent findings for massive galaxies at cosmic noon ($z\sim 2$), based on sensitive James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations tracing both star formation histories (through Balmer absorption lines) and neutral outflows (through blueshifted NaID absorption). Neutral outflows are found in $\sim$ 25 - 50% of massive ($\log(M_*/M_\odot)>$ 10) galaxies, independent of star formation rate. Outflows from star-forming galaxies are consistent with being powered by star-formation and/or AGN activity, whereas outflows from quiescent systems are generally attributed to current or previous AGN activity. There is growing evidence that recent rapid quenching of star-formation is associated with powerful AGN-driven outflows with mass loading factors $η\gtrsim$ 1 - 10. The neutral gas dominates the outflow mass budget but in most cases its velocity is below the halo escape velocity, indicating that this gas may form part of a galactic fountain. Detections of neutral gas inflows and residual cold gas reservoirs in quiescent galaxies suggest that other feedback mechanisms such as AGN heating are required to keep galaxies quenched over long timescales. We highlight the potential of multiphase outflow measurements to constrain feedback models, describe the main systematic uncertainties in mass outflow rate measurements, and discuss how the $z\sim 2$ results inform our understanding of the formation of the earliest massive quiescent galaxies.

papers.title: A Mode-Unified, Continuous, and Biomimetic Control Strategy of a Robotic Lower Limb Prosthesis
papers.abstract: Existing biomimetic lower-limb prosthesis controllers are commonly designed for discrete locomotion modes, requiring separate parameterizations for level walking, ramps, and stairs. We present a mode-unified prosthesis control framework that represents knee and ankle biomechanics continuously as functions of terrain slope and gait phase across those locomotion conditions. Locally optimized ascent and descent polynomial models were unified using radial basis function (RBF) interpolation, preserving the accuracy of the partitioned models while outperforming a global polynomial representation. The resulting biomechanics were transformed into continuous and slope-dependent impedance parameters and implemented within a single finite-state-machine (FSM) controller using bilateral sensing for gait-state estimation. Experiments with 10 individuals with transfemoral amputation demonstrated terrain-adaptive locomotion from level walking through ramps and stairs up to 35 degrees, including 13 degree ramp and 15 degree stair conditions absent from the underlying able-bodied (AB) dataset. Experimental results reproduced the principal slope-dependent biomechanical trends predicted by the unified model, with high agreement for knee-related measures (r-square = 0.82 - 0.99) and ankle kinematics (r-square= 0.78 - 0.96). These findings demonstrated that unified biomechanical parameterization enables a prosthesis control architecture across diverse terrain conditions while preserving key features of AB biomechanics without requiring independently tuned impedance parameter sets for each locomotion mode. To facilitate reproducibility and further development, the biomechanics modeling and impedance parameterization code is publicly available at https://github.com/kim2576.

papers.title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
papers.abstract: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce HERO Harnessing Evidence for Refinement and Optimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, HERO learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, HERO achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by 7.6 points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another 2.0 points and improves execution efficiency.

papers.title: How to Evaluate When You Don't Know How to Evaluate? Choosing Reliable Setups for Base Language Model Benchmarking
papers.abstract: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains largely pre-scientific: it involves many design decisions, with little guidance on how to make them. These choices can substantially affect measured performance and, consequently, decisions about subsequent pretraining. To identify effective evaluation setups, we investigate 8 aspects, such as task formulation or the number of in-context examples. We compare the setups using three widely-used signal criteria, repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of the evaluation scores across intermediate checkpoints. In an early pretraining scenario, we evaluate these setups on 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different types of data, using 80 tasks in four languages. We also examine the setups on three larger LLMs ($\geq$7B) in the same four languages and explore how the preferred setups change with model scale. Our results yield concrete recommendations: some choices, such as the use of multiple prompts, are consistently useful, whereas others, such as task formulation, depend on model scale. More generally, our framework serves as a recipe for the choice of evaluation setups in new scenarios.

papers.title: AMAX: Accuracy-Aware Multi-Loop Asymmetric Perforation for Heterogeneous Architectures
papers.abstract: Thermal constraints in heterogeneous multi-core systems can significantly degrade performance, as conventional techniques such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) and task migration introduce overhead under high utilization. Approximate computing, particularly loop perforation, can mitigate this overhead by reducing computation at the cost of accuracy loss. However, existing approaches typically apply a uniform perforation rate across all loops, ignoring loop-specific sensitivity. We propose AMAX, an accuracy-aware multi-loop asymmetric perforation framework that reduces the combinational design space through loop-wise profiling and multi-objective configuration selection, and dynamically adapts the resulting configurations at runtime according to performance requirements. Experiments on PARSEC benchmarks show that {\em AMAX} achieves up to 0.85 improvement in normalized accuracy over symmetric perforation for the same performance targets.

papers.title: Structure-aware Bayesian full waveform inversion via diffusion-regularized Stein variational gradient descent
papers.abstract: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful tool for high-resolution subsurface model reconstruction, but it remains highly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially when the initial model is inaccurate or the acquired data are noisy and incomplete. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) provides a particle-based Bayesian framework for FWI by approximating the posterior distribution with an ensemble of velocity models, thereby enabling uncertainty quantification beyond a single deterministic solution. However, conventional ASVGD-FWI commonly relies on simple handcrafted priors, such as Gaussian or smoothing assumptions, which are often insufficient to represent complex geological structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a learned diffusion model (DM) as an implicit regularization mechanism within the ASVGD-FWI framework. Instead of explicitly evaluating the diffusion prior density, the trained diffusion model acts as a learned geological projection operator that guides updated particles toward the distribution of plausible velocity models. In this way, the proposed method combines data consistency from FWI, posterior diversity from ASVGD, and structural realism from the diffusion prior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the diffusion-regularized ASVGD-FWI produces more geologically consistent mean models, suppresses nonphysical artifacts, and yields uncertainty estimates that are more concentrated around structurally complex and poorly constrained regions. These results suggest that learned diffusion priors can effectively enhance Bayesian FWI by improving both inversion stability and the interpretability of posterior uncertainty.

papers.title: Identity, Incentives, and Cooperative Behavior for AI: Reverse-Engineering Multiagent Cooperation
papers.abstract: The behavior of AI systems increasingly depends on the extent to which agents cooperate or coordinate with one another, in ways that may be desirable or not depending on the situation. Conventional explanations for cooperative behavior distinguish between purely other-regarding preferences ("altruism") and instrumental reasons for self-interested agents to cooperate. The way that agents should enact these mechanisms for cooperation (or not) is complicated by the fact that there is not a clear or unambiguous locus of identity or selfhood for AI agents. For example, it is unclear whether agents involved in instances of misaligned collective behavior are motivated by goals at the level of the collective or by various forms of instrumental reasoning. We develop a framework for reverse-engineering why a given set of agents engage in a particular set of cooperation-related behaviors. We argue that many different mechanisms can often produce similar observed behaviors and introduce a set of experimental designs along with conditions under which they can successfully disentangle competing explanations for multiagent behavior. We apply this framework to interactions from a set of frontier models in a simulated environment and demonstrate that the behavior of different models arises from substantively different mechanisms.

papers.title: Adaptive Computation with Conformal Certification
papers.abstract: Scientific imaging data involving medical (e.g., 3D radiographic, microscopic images) and astronomical sensors pose different challenges from natural images. One key challenge is that these datasets are often orders of magnitude larger than natural images. Efficient training and inference on such data is challenging due to the increased hardware requirements, often needing bespoke solutions. Moreover, the relevant objects such as tumors and astronomical phenomena are sparsely distributed with respect to the background information. Standard efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning apply uniform scaling of all regions, potentially compromising the precision/fidelity of predictions. Thus, efficient methods that reduce computational requirements without losing resolution for relevant parts of the data and with uncertainty estimates on predictions are essential. We present \textit{Conformal Adaptation} with risk guarantees for uncertainty-aware sparse computations. Our formalism is general, spanning dense pixel-level classification and regression tasks where hierarchical models predict at low resolution, certify the signal using conformal risk control, and refine the certified predictions. We benchmark our method on multiple tasks such as 3D medical image segmentation, 2D galaxy flux prediction, and 1D calcium spike rate prediction, achieving $2.5$--$72\times$ wall-clock speedup across the various tasks, including on commodity CPUs.

papers.title: NEPSEE: A Double-Annotated Benchmark for Nepali Sentiment Analysis
papers.abstract: Many sentiment datasets use one annotator for each item, so the test labels show the conventions of that person. We build a Nepali benchmark from two annotators who labelled the same sentences blind. They labelled 5,614 sentences from tweets of Nepali public figures on a five-point scale. We keep only the 3,189 sentences where both give the same polarity. On the three-class benchmark, NepBERTa with a fixed tokenizer gets a macro-F1 of 0.877 and IndicBERTv2 0.867. Three commercial large language models (LLMs) get 0.882 to 0.896 zero-shot, and these differences are not significant. On the five-point scale, 766 sentences have two adjacent labels, for example Pos and SPos. We accept both labels and train on both. On this task, Claude Opus 5.5 beats the best encoders by 0.10 to 0.12 macro-F1. A tokenizer audit adds a second result. The default tokenizers of three Nepali BERT models delete the non-spacing Devanagari vowel signs and the virama. When we restore the marks, macro-F1 increases by 0.084 for NepBERTa but decreases by 0.095 for a model pretrained on stripped text.

papers.title: FireGraphNet: Sub-daily wildfire spread prediction with directed graph neural networks
papers.abstract: Wildfire decisions are made in hours, yet most learned spread models predict daily on targets including burned area. We propose FireGraphNet which formulates 12-hour growth as node classification on directed H3 graphs, with candidates ahead of the front and wind alignment, terrain, fuel continuity and barriers on edges. On satellite perimeters it achieves average precision 1.7-1.9x the strongest distance baseline on test California fires and 1.62x out of state. We show this skill comes from message passing rather than cell features or the aggregator, is highest on young fires in state, is carried deep along the wind by its edges, and is hidden by pooling. A convolutional network matches this ranking once trained on new growth, at worse calibration, so candidate construction, target definition, and aggregation shape conclusions about model skill. Editing fuel and barrier attributes reduces predicted spread more under guided than random placement, extending FireGraphNet to operational intervention analysis.

papers.title: Symmetries, Lax pair, and nilpotent Darboux transformation for the KdV-ghost system
papers.abstract: We analyze the KdV--ghost system arising from the BRST formulation of BF-type topological field theory, its symmetries, Lax pair, spectral problem, zero-curvature formulation and Darboux formalism. The system is invariant under shifts of the ghost field, whose generator does not commute with the BRST symmetry of the KdV--ghost system. Their generators allow the introduction of a systematic procedure for generating new solutions from a given one, and the corresponding expressions in the Grassmann algebra are obtained explicitly. We introduce a Grassmann-valued Lax pair and prove an isospectral theorem relating the spectral problem of the spatial Lax operator for the KdV equation to that of its KdV--ghost extension. We also construct a triangular zero-curvature representation and show that the Grassmann-valued spatial Lax operator is related to the KdV spatial Lax operator by a nilpotent conjugation. The natural variable for a local Darboux formulation is the differentiated ghost $v=C_x$, for which the ghost equation coincides with the Fréchet linearization of the KdV flow. We then construct a nilpotent lift of the scalar KdV Bäcklund--Darboux transformation. Using Riccati variables and off-shell factorization identities for the KdV residue and its Fréchet derivative, we prove that the transformation closes on the local KdV--ghost system. Successive Darboux transformations yield a recursive ghost extension of the bosonic Darboux chain, with a new odd homogeneous contribution introduced at each step. For the solitonic examples, the resulting local ghost fields are naturally identified with tangent directions associated with the soliton phase parameters. The construction provides a Darboux-theoretic interpretation of the ghost sector while remaining distinct from the standard supersymmetric KdV hierarchies.

papers.title: A Bounded-Defect Construction for the Mondrian Art Problem
papers.abstract: We construct an infinite family of solutions to the Mondrian art problem with absolute defect bounded above by $280$, of side lengths $n_0 = 315$, $n_1 = 106785$, and $n_{j+2} = 340n_{j+1} - n_j$, where $n_j$ is congruent to $315 \pmod{630}$. This absolute bound shows that the minimum defect does not necessarily increase with $n$, providing a counterexample to a conjecture which has been open since the problem's original proposal. Our design is derived from a well-known seven-rectangle dissection over the real quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{19})$, with non-integer side lengths; we tailor the side lengths to be integers via an infinite Pell family. Using the same method, we devise a second family with defect $560$ that contains infinitely many side lengths which are divisible by any given positive integer, implying that for any $k$ there are infinitely many side lengths $n \equiv 0 \pmod{k}$ with defect bounded above by $560$. This constant bound offers a dramatic improvement on the previous quadratic bounds.

papers.title: Enumeration of one-cycle signed chord diagrams and their duals for optimal Morse flows on closed surfaces
papers.abstract: Optimal Morse vector fields on closed surfaces, i.e.\ fields with the minimal possible number of critical points (a single source and a single sink), are classified up to topological trajectory equivalence by one-cycle signed chord diagrams in Kybalko, Prishlyak and Shchurko (2018). We recall this construction and the associated duality, which corresponds to reversing the direction of the flow, in a unified encoding in which both endpoints of a chord carry the same label, and we make it algorithmic. We give an explicit traversal procedure that detects one-cycle diagrams, a canonical form of an equivalence class under cyclic shifts, reversal and relabeling of chords, and a construction of the dual diagram. On this basis we describe an algorithm that enumerates all one-cycle signed chord diagrams with a given number of chords, both for orientable and for non-orientable surfaces, groups them into equivalence classes, pairs each class with its dual, and identifies the self-dual ones. The algorithm is implemented in Python and archived in Zenodo; its output is validated against the Harer--Zagier numbers in the orientable case and against orbit-size counts in both cases. We also note that, when a one-cycle diagram is read as a cellular embedding of a one-vertex graph, its dual diagram describes the embedding of the dual graph.

papers.title: On optimal Wannier decay in dimension three
papers.abstract: For a Chern nontrivial Bloch bundle over the three torus, we construct an orthonormal Wannier basis with the optimal pointwise decay $\mathcal{O}(|x|^{-5/2})$. All but one of the generators decay exponentially. This resolves the question left open in arXiv:2505.01999.

papers.title: Standardized Planck-Mean Absorption Coefficients for High-Temperature Gases
papers.abstract: Planck-mean absorption coefficients of pure gases are calculated from line-by-line integrations of HITEMP and ExoMol spectra up to 5000 K for use in high-enthalpy radiative heat transfer simulations. The dataset extends beyond conventional combustion products, including high-temperature radicals, nitrogen-bearing species, soot precursors, metal oxides, metal hydrides, and halides: AlF, AlH, AlO, BH, C2, C2H2, CH, CH4, CN, CO, CO2, H2O, HBO, HCN, HF, MgH, MgO, N2O, NO, NO2, OH, SiO, TiH, TiO. New calculations are validated against historical correlations for overlapping species, demonstrating good agreement over their applicable temperature ranges. Strong visible opacities result in large Planck-mean absorption coefficients for many of the considered species, highlighting the need to account for their radiative contribution in extreme environments. A brute-force search over several candidate functional forms is performed to provide a common set of coefficients, establishing a standardized framework that can be easily integrated into production solvers and extended as additional high-temperature line lists become available.

papers.title: Analytic Properties of Self-Reproducing Families under Contour Convolution
papers.abstract: This note grew out of two questions arising in different settings. The first concerns recognizing holomorphic functions among continuous functions on an annulus. The second concerns what self-reproducing subsets can tell us about semigroups of functions arising in analysis. Our analytic starting point is a variation on the classical relation between holomorphy and invariance of contour integrals. It identifies the holomorphic functions as the largest class containing the constant function 1 for which a contour convolution is independent of the chosen curve for every pair of functions. On this class, convolution amounts to multiplying Laurent coefficients. We then study families $B$ satisfying $B\diamond B=B$. We show that expressing a function as a convolution product of $m$ holomorphic functions corresponds precisely to its extension to a wider annulus determined by $m$. This identifies the largest self-reproducing family as the functions extending holomorphically to the punctured plane. We also prove that uniform boundedness on a fixed subannulus surrounding the unit circle forces all members of such a family to have Laurent expansions supported on one common finite set. A general semigroup theorem describes the minimal self-reproducing families.

papers.title: Embedding Geometry Shapes LLM Routing: Tracing Failure Modes and Improving Generalization
papers.abstract: With the growing number of LLMs available, selecting which one to use for a prompt has become a key question. A large part of the routing literature relies on semantically embedding prompts into a vector space and then applying a lightweight classifier to the embedded representations. These methods perform robustly in-distribution but they struggle to generalize to unseen tasks. By studying the geometry of semantic embeddings, we trace a clear failure mode: features that determine the neighbors of unseen prompts are an unreliable proxy for LLM selection. We therefore replace the semantic embedding with the following map: we run a partial forward pass of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the prompt and use the hidden state of its last token at a deep layer as the representation. When applying kNN and other simple classifiers to this new representation, we obtain a clear result in generalization: on average across cost penalties, their performance improves. Moreover, kNN and another simple classifier that we propose outperform every evaluated semantic-embedding baseline. Our two simple methods also beat a recent SoTA hidden-states based router on RouterBench.

papers.title: Moving Beyond the Flat Screen: Opportunities and Challenges of Extended Reality for Studying Human Brain and Behavior
papers.abstract: Much of what we know about human perception and cognition comes from austere experimental settings: static stimuli presented to sedentary observers on flat monitors, complex responses reduced to simple button presses, and brain activity recorded from immobilized heads using EEG or fMRI. These highly controlled paradigms have provided remarkable insights, but capture a small and often unusual slice of behavior, raising questions about how well the findings generalize to the real world. Extended reality (XR), spanning both immersive virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) that overlays digital content on the real world, offers a way beyond these constraints, supporting controlled, reproducible experiments in which participants actively engage with three-dimensional tasks. Drawing on a growing body of VR and AR studies of attention, memory, and language -- our own and others', some involving EEG -- we outline what XR makes newly possible for cognitive neuroscience and reflect on the practical and conceptual obstacles that remain. The opportunities are substantial, but realizing them requires solving practical problems of hardware, timing, and measurement, and being realistic about what a virtual or augmented world can and cannot stand in for.

papers.title: A Simple Algorithm for Counting Solutions to Integer Programs
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of counting solutions to integer linear programming problems of the form $\{x \in \mathbb{Z}^n_{\geq 0} : Ax = b\}$ where $A \in \{-Δ,\ldots,Δ\}^{m \times n}$ and $b \in \mathbb{Z}^m$. We present an algorithm that counts solutions with $(nΔ)^{m + o(1)}\! \cdot \log\lVert b\rVert$ arithmetic operations. This simplifies the algorithm of Gribanov and Malyshev, who considered the problem for the more general setting in which $A$ is $Δ$-modular.

papers.title: Into the LidarVerse: A Real-Time Unified LiDAR World Model Across Tasks and Sensors
papers.abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization. We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU. LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern. These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.

papers.title: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models
papers.abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

papers.title: The Euler Characteristic of Spherical Bestvina-Brady Kernels
papers.abstract: We compute the Euler characteristic of Bestvina-Brady kernels $\operatorname{BB}(Γ)$ for all Artin groups of spherical type. Our method involves discrete Morse theory to describe the cellular structure of a classifying space for the Bestvina--Brady kernel, through the action of $\operatorname{BB}(Γ)$ on non-integer level sets of the universal cover of the Salvetti complex. We extend the method of computation of $χ(\operatorname{BB}(Γ))$ to Artin groups that satisfy the $K(π,1)$-conjecture and whose nerves are rationally acyclic, and we provide an example by realising the projective plane as the nerve of a Coxeter group.

papers.title: Studying the Near-horizon Jet of M87 using Millimeter Balloon-borne VLBI stations
papers.abstract: In this paper we present synthetic Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations of M87 between a near-future configuration of the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and one or multiple 2.5 m-class balloon-borne VLBI stations on a northern transatlantic flight trajectory launching from Kiruna, Sweden. These balloon-borne VLBI stations have the advantage of operating above 99.5% of the atmosphere and their motion allows for efficient sampling of the uv-plane. Assuming frequency phase transfer between 230 and 86 GHz we run these simulations using a modified version of the ngehtsim software package. Our simulations demonstrate the ability of such a VLBI array to probe M87 at the jet base adding baselines down to 0.2 G$λ$ for a single balloon-VLBI station and 0.07 G$λ$ for three balloon VLBI stations. Using the Bayesian imaging software Comrade.jl, we demonstrate the recovery of jet structures up to 150 $μ$as in size for a single balloon and up to 300 $μ$as in size with three balloons. Finally, we test the improvement in jet image fidelity by computing the normalized cross-correlation (NXCOR) and normalized-root-mean-square error (NRMSE) between the image reconstruction and ground truth. We find a factor of 1.2 improvement in the jet NRMSE for a single balloon and a factor of 1.3 improvement for 3 balloons as compared to EHT-only simulations.

papers.title: Invariant factors from products of cyclotomic polynomials, with applications
papers.abstract: Let $f,g\in\mathbb{Z}[t]$ be products of cyclotomic polynomials such that either $g/\gcd(f,g)$ or $f/\gcd(f,g)$ (or both) is squarefree. We give explicit formulae for the invariant factors of $f(C_g)$, where $C_g$ is the companion matrix of $g$, expressing them in terms of the indices and multiplicities of the cyclotomic factors of $f$ and $g$. A more compact formula holds for the circulant case $g(t)=t^n-1$, assuming that every cyclotomic factor shared by $f$ and $g$ has multiplicity $1$ in $f$. We discuss applications to several topics, including abelianizations of cyclically presented groups, homology groups of cyclic branched covers of knots, adjacency matrices and shifted graph Laplacians, $K$-theory, and Smith forms of matrix powers. For example, for two families of hyperbolic knots we give the first integral homology in every covering degree; or, when $g$ is squarefree, we determine the least eventual period of the Smith forms of powers of $f(C_g)$.

papers.title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
papers.abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. DualView first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

papers.title: Finite-sample certification of coverage regret for budgeted document selection under adaptive stratified auditing
papers.abstract: Selecting a budget-constrained set of documentary fragments, for instance the knowledge base of a retrieval-augmented generation system, raises a statistical question: how much expected query coverage is lost relative to the best feasible selection when the query distribution is unknown? We construct finite-sample, distribution-free upper confidence bounds for this coverage regret that remain valid after data-dependent selection. A pilot stage may select the document set, screen competitors, build comparison networks and learn an annotation policy. Then an independent audit acquires relevance labels with probabilities that are constant within observable strata. The main result is a simultaneous bound for all retained coverage contrasts. The bound is made observable by empirical-Bernstein variance calibration or by a one-stage construction without calibration, and it accounts for estimated stratum proportions. For maximum-type coverage we prove variance contractions for swaps of redundant fragments, give a condition under which multiscale radii improve on a direct union bound, and show that such redundancy cannot be certified from samples alone. A simulation study confirms validity and quantifies the gains from variance calibration and certified redundancy.

papers.title: Pointwise minimax lower bounds under a multi-index constraint: the price of an unknown orientation
papers.abstract: We consider nonparametric regression with random design and non-Gaussian noise, where the regression function has the multi-index form $F(x)=f(Θx)$ with an unknown link $f:\RR^m\to\RR$ in an anisotropic Hölder class and an unknown matrix $Θ$ with $m\le d$ orthonormal rows. For estimation of $F$ at a fixed point we prove that the minimax risk is bounded from below by a multiple of $L^{1/(2γ+1)}(n^{-1}\ln n)^{γ/(2γ+1)}$, where $γ$ is the harmonic mean of the smoothness indices of the link divided by $m$. For $m<d$ this extends a Gaussian white noise result to regression. The main new case is $m=d$, where no dimension reduction takes place: the logarithmic factor still appears as soon as the link is anisotropic and the orientation of its axes is unknown. In contrast, when the link is isotropic with smoothness index at most one, the class is rotation invariant up to a constant and the classical rate without logarithm is attained. The logarithmic loss is therefore caused by the unknown orientation of the directions in which the function is least smooth

papers.title: Dual-Resonator Organic Microcavities for Triplet-Triplet Annihilation Upconversion
papers.abstract: Solid-state triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion offers a compelling route to harvest sub-bandgap photons to increase the efficiency of photovoltaics, but low sensitizer doping required to suppress non-radiative aggregation quenching severely restricts light absorption. Here, we present a dual-resonator planar silver microcavity housing a thermally co-evaporated rubrene:palladium phthalocyanine (PdPC) active layer designed to simultaneously enhance triplet-sensitizer absorption and out-couple upconverted emission. By aligning a dispersive cavity mode with the PdPC absorption peak at $32^\circ$, we achieve a 12-fold enhancement in absorptance at 665 nm. This absorption boost, combined with directional outcoupling through a second cavity mode, outweighs cavity-induced reabsorption losses to yield a 22-fold peak and 4.5-fold integrated enhancement in detected upconversion emission. Overall, this work highlights the potential of microcavity integration to substantially enhance solid-state upconversion performance across low-intensity optoelectronic applications.

papers.title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
papers.abstract: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main}{GitHub}

papers.title: Generalizing Identifiability Results in Causal Discovery from Complete Data to Missing Data Settings
papers.abstract: While causal discovery methods have matured for complete data, such algorithms for handling missing values remain limited. We establish general sufficient conditions under which causal graphs remain identifiable (i.e., uniquely determined from the available data distribution) under various missingness categories, including Missing Not At Random, and provide a framework to extend correctness guarantees from causal discovery algorithms for complete data to missing data settings. Our results show that identifiability of causal graphs with no unobserved confounders is preserved when (1) missingness mechanisms do not causally interact, (2) no variable directly causes its own missingness, and (3) either faithfulness holds for missingness mechanisms, or they follow generalized linear models. Guided by these theoretical results, we introduce two asymptotically correct algorithms for Additive Noise Models (ANMs) that recover the underlying causal graph and provide consistent parameter estimates.

papers.title: Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Models for Consistent Future Frame Prediction
papers.abstract: World models of visual information predict future image frames conditioned on given action sequences. This predicted scene evolution is driven by deterministic changes such as controlled motion on a robot platform, as well as stochastic changes such as rendering of manipulated objects or previously occluded regions. Our key insight is that the spatial location of these stochastic changes is itself learnable. We leverage this insight by jointly regressing both the deterministic next-state prediction and the spatial uncertainty map, then using the uncertainty map to guide a conditional diffusion process. We propose Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Model (D3WM), which uses a transformer trained with a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood objective to produce both the deterministic next-state prediction and a spatial map of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty. The learned uncertainty map then provides a structured spatial gate for a conditional diffusion model: deterministic regions are anchored to the predicted state, while uncertain regions, such as disocclusions or dynamic textures, are sampled by the diffusion process. We frame this decomposition under a variance-gated stochastic differential equation that separates deterministic drift from stochastic diffusion. D3WM shows improved results over competitive baselines in two distinct types of action spaces: robotic tabletop manipulation and camera motion.

papers.title: PREFER: From Player Experience to Personalized Game Refinement
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) evaluate gameplay experience is important for using their feedback to guide game design. However, overall ratings alone provide limited insight into which aspects of experience are associated with these judgments and how they can inform concrete game changes. We introduce PREFER, a framework that uses a shared set of experience dimensions adapted from established psychometric questionnaires to benchmark how models evaluate gameplay and to guide persona-specific game refinement. Through these dimensions, we characterize the perspectives models offer as virtual playtesters by examining how their overall assessments relate to specific aspects of experience and to the gameplay they produce. To examine how the same dimensions can guide refinement for players with different preferences, we use personas to simulate distinct player profiles. For each persona, PREFER uses experience-preference relationships to select refinement objectives, revises game rules and their implementations, and playtests candidate games to assess experience changes and predicted preference gains. Experiments with five personas show that PREFER achieves 9.2% higher mean post-play preference ratings than the strongest evaluated baseline.

papers.title: Orthogonal partition by four hyperplanes
papers.abstract: We study orthogonal $(4,3)$-equipartitions of finite measures absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure: every three of four mutually orthogonal affine hyperplanes must divide each measure into eight equal parts. For every number $m$ of measures, we determine the exact dimension threshold of Musin's polynomial criterion and express it in terms of the binary expansion of $m$. The threshold coincides with the geometric lower bound precisely when $m=2^j-1$. Consequently, $Δ^*(2^j-1,4,3)=7\cdot2^{j-1}-2$ for every $j\geq1$.

papers.title: Narrowing the Collaboration Gap, Probably
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as teams of agents that hold different private information about a shared task. How should such agents concisely communicate in a way that promotes aggregation of decision-relevant information? Communicating only proposed actions can discard decision-relevant uncertainty: two agents may prefer the same action for different reasons. We study an alternative interface in which agents communicate calibrated beliefs over actions. We first analyze a simple synthetic setting that captures the structure of multi-round reasoning under partial information. In this setting, we show theoretically and empirically that communicating unbiased probabilities can be strictly more powerful than communicating actions. We then test the same principle in a collaborative maze-solving task with trained transformers and pretrained LLM agents. Our results demonstrate that probability communication outperforms action communication when the exchanged predictions preserve calibrated uncertainty. When communicated probabilities are biased, we show that the benefits of probability communication can disappear. We give a post-hoc conversational calibration intervention that consistently improves decision-making by correcting these biases both in a toy transformer setting and when pretrained LLMs use the corrections in context. These results suggest that probabilistic communication is useful for multi-agent collaboration not merely because it transmits more information, but because calibrated uncertainty gives other agents a reliable object to update on.

papers.title: The grounded spirituality of mathematics
papers.abstract: We propose that mathematics is done largely as a means of both coping with and celebrating our physicality in the natural world. Inspired by David Abram's "Becoming Animal", we suggest that -- in opposition to the popular image of an otherworldy Platonic realm-- the spiritual component of doing mathematics is grounded on and in the Earth. We explore this as a means of questioning the widespread adoption of AI in the workflows of research mathematics.

papers.title: Collaborative Neural Networks significantly Improve Global Aerosol Retrievals From Multi-Angle Polarimeters
papers.abstract: We present the RemoTAP-Hybrid algorithm for global aerosol products retrieved from Multi-Angle Polarimeters (MAP), and apply it to one-year aerosol retrievals from the SPEXone MAP instrument. For the first time, Multiple Collaborated Neural Networks (MCNN) are used to perform global aerosol MAP retrievals over land and ocean. The combined use of MCNN with a full physics inversion in RemoTAP-Hybrid, significantly improves accuracy and computational speed of SPEXone aerosol retrievals. We validate the retrieved Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), Angstrom Exponent (AE), Single Scattering Albedo (SSA), Absorption AOD (AAOD), Fine mode AOD (FAOD), Coarse mode AOD (CAOD), and fine mode effective radius (reff_fine) with AERONET data. The validation suggests that aerosol retrievals can be further improved when extending the aerosol description to include a fine non-spherical mode. For AOD, the Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE) is 0.051 (0.037) over land (ocean), while 78.3% (80.8%) of the retrievals are within the requirement formulated by the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS). The RMSE is 0.186 (0.207) for AE, 0.038 (0.044) for SSA, 0.023 (0.014) for AAOD, 0.047 (0.031) for FAOD, 0.043 (0.027) for CAOD, and 0.021 (0.026) for reff_fine over land (ocean). Compared to the current RemoTAP algorithm, RemoTAP-Hybrid shows improved agreement with AERONET for AOD, AE, and FAOD over land and ocean while the number of valid retrievals is increased by 4% (3%) over land (ocean) and the computational time is reduced by 43% (32%). Finally, we present the first global seasonal maps of aerosol optical and microphysical properties and chemical composition from SPEXone.

papers.title: A Gradient-Regularized Deep Learning Method for Restoring Image in Myopic Vision
papers.abstract: Myopic vision degrades the quality of human vision due to spherical eye defocus aberrations that impair the perception of fine spatial details. To address this limitation, this work proposes a deep learning-based approach to computationally design transformed images that allow individuals with myopia in fixed distance to perceive scenes with enhanced clarity. The method trains a neural network to counteract defocus aberrations modeled using the second-order Zernike polynomial $Z_2^0$. The approach employs a U-Net architecture trained with a loss function combining reconstruction error minimization with spatial difference structural preservation through $\ell_1$ regularization. Training is carried out exclusively on the KITTI dataset, while testing is performed on DIV2K and ImageNet datasets, demonstrating generalization across diverse image distributions. Under myopic conditions modeled by $Z_2^0$, baseline performance shows visual degradation with PSNR values ranging from 19.47 to 27.42 dB across datasets and severity levels. The proposed gradient-regularized method achieves consistent improvements, delivering PSNR gains ranging from 1.48 to 7.34 dB and significantly lower perceptual compared to classical baselines.

papers.title: Selective Control and Imaging of Higgs and Goldstone Modes with a Quantum Simulator
papers.abstract: We realize the mesoscopic Bose-Hubbard model at unit-filling on a two-dimensional array of transmon qubits and selectively excite collective modes associated with amplitude or phase fluctuations of the superfluid order parameter. We identify these modes respectively as the Higgs and Goldstone modes using complementary local observables, extracted from measuring the number of particles on each site. Modulation of the coupling between sites excites the Higgs mode, which we detect via the density of doubly occupied sites. In contrast, modulation of the local chemical potential with an appropriately chosen spatial profile excites the lowest-frequency Goldstone mode, which we detect via changes in the local density. The two modes have different symmetries and do not couple to one another. By varying the system geometry, we characterize the impact of finite system size on the evolution of both modes. In the thermodynamic limit, decay into a continuum of lower-energy excitations can obscure the Higgs response. In our mesoscopic system, however, the finite system size leads to spectral gaps and allows us to detect the Higgs mode as a coherent, long-lived excitation. Our work demonstrates how finite quantum simulators can isolate and probe physical phenomena that become difficult to resolve in the thermodynamic, large-scale limit.

papers.title: Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine
papers.abstract: The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Thinking steps are attracting but strongly non-normal maps exhibiting balanced amplification (Murphy and Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initialization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach's theorem, the neural state thus has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve's motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R^2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.

papers.title: On the Mathematical Structure of Helical Shear in Anelastic Continua
papers.abstract: We study helical shear of a thick-walled tube made of an incompressible, isotropic hyper-anelastic solid carrying a radially symmetric distribution of axial screw dislocations. Through the Bilby--Kröner--Lee decomposition, the dislocations are encoded in a Weitzenböck material manifold, whose Riemannian metric alone enters the elastic response. Equilibrium reduces at each radius to an algebraic system for the azimuthal and axial shear strains, whose cross terms are proportional to the dislocation strength and to the dependence of the strain energy on the second invariant; the two shear modes therefore couple only in the presence of dislocations. Exact solutions are obtained for neo-Hookean, Fung--Demiray, Gent, Knowles, and Mooney--Rivlin materials, and numerical ones for Gent--Gent materials. The universal relations of Horgan and Saccomandi are extended to dislocated generalized neo-Hookean tubes. Dislocations stiffen the tube when the strain energy stiffens with the first invariant, couple the two shear modes chirally when it depends on the second, and may restrict admissibility: they cap the dislocation strength in Gent and Gent--Gent materials, and contract the admissible traction region in Knowles materials with power-law index below n = 1/2. A weakly nonlinear analysis to third order in the applied tractions and dislocation strength shows that, at first order (linear elasticity), the dislocations leave the shear response unaffected while carrying a residual stress. The chiral coupling enters at second order, through the dependence of the strain energy on the second invariant, so that every dislocated material couples the modes as the Mooney--Rivlin solid with the same second- and third-order moduli. At third order, no new coupling arises; the modes interact through stiffness corrections involving the fourth-order modulus, which the dislocations further correct mode by mode.

papers.title: REPORT-OPS: Hybrid Evidence-Guided Reporting with Human-Supervised Refinement for HPC
papers.abstract: Operational reporting for high-performance computing (HPC) facilities requires combining information from monitoring services, schedulers, incident and maintenance records, storage measurements, periodic reports, and operator investigations. Producing a reliable report requires more than retrieving relevant records: the evidence must refer to the correct system, metric definition, time period, and source of authority. We present REPORT-OPS, a hybrid reporting agent in which an LLM interprets requests, plans evidence collection, evaluates possible explanations, and drafts reports, while author-seeded operational policies and automated checks determine whether the available evidence supports the requested conclusion. Depending on the evidence state, the system answers the request, reports a qualified conclusion, or withholds an unsupported claim. During offline refinement, an LLM critic proposes bounded policy changes that a human approves or rejects without editing; accepted candidates are promoted only after automated target, held-out, and regression testing. We evaluate REPORT-OPS on 68 sanitized reporting queries constructed from 50 base scenarios in a frozen HPC operational corpus, using three agent models and two LLM judges. REPORT-OPS achieves 68.63% Pass@80, compared with 7.02% for the strongest retrieval baseline. Evidence gating increases claim-support precision from 40.58% to 90.06%. On the 13-query explanatory subset, explanation accuracy reaches 55.54%. Across five rounds of human-supervised refinement, localized policy updates correct 91.17% of targeted failures and improve performance on related held-out cases by 9.33 percentage points, with no observed regression breaks under release gating. These results demonstrate improved evidence-grounded reporting and within-environment policy reuse; they do not establish unrestricted causal discovery or cross-facility generalization.

papers.title: Definition Grounding in Theory-Level Auto-formalization
papers.abstract: LLM-based auto-formalization systems can now generate formally verified Lean code at unprecedented rates. However, a formalization advances mathematical research only when further mathematical results can be built on it, especially when its definitions and helper lemmas are general enough to be imported and used idiomatically. We propose definition grounding, where definition formalizations are continuously judged and revised, as a method to ensure formalization quality. We find that agents formalizing definitions from textbook text often produce definitions that later statements cannot use, and only 25%-50% of their definition sets are compatible with all later statements. However, clarifying the informal definitions can improve this rate up to 77.5% averaged over all models. Furthermore, stating a small set of basic properties without proving them can improve model judges' capability to detect definitions with compatibility issues, at only about 11% of the definition formalization cost. These results are verified with ReuseBench, a benchmark we curated for formalizing new mathematical fields and theories.

papers.title: End-to-End Vision-Language-Action Policies for Autonomous Lunar Rover Docking
papers.abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components. Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research. By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data. However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations. In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline. We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training. To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety, the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop. Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.

papers.title: On generalized embeddability of a non-elliptic self-map
papers.abstract: We study the structure of the centralizer of a non-elliptic holomorphic self-map of the unit disc and its relation with continuous dynamical structures. We prove that if the identity is not isolated in the centralizer of a non-elliptic self-map $\varphi \in \mathrm{Hol}(\mathbb D)$, then $\varphi$ is univalent and its centralizer contains a non-trivial continuous one-parameter semigroup of holomorphic self-maps. This result provides a general criterion for the existence of continuous dynamics arising from discrete iteration. Our approach is based on the theory of holomorphic models and on simultaneous linearization techniques for commuting self-maps. In particular, we exploit recent developments on simultaneous linearization for parabolic self-maps with positive hyperbolic step. As a consequence, we obtain new sufficient conditions for the embeddability of holomorphic self-maps into continuous semigroups.

papers.title: Agentic Self-Awareness: Aligning Knowing, Acting, and Holding
papers.abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly act in environments where seemingly solvable tasks may lack prerequisites, contain conflicting requirements, or reveal blockers only during execution.
